vaisakhi.s: Vaisakhi, or Baisakhi, is a spring harvest festival of the Punjab and one of the most important festivals of the Sikh calendar, commemorating the founding of the Khalsa. In 1801, on the day of Vaisakhi, Ranjit Singh was proclaimed Maharaja of the Punjab at Lahore.

vaishali.s: Vaishali was an ancient city in the north of present-day Bihar in eastern India, associated with the early Buddhist and Jain traditions. In the Gupta period it was an important urban centre.

vakil.s: Vakil was a Persian title meaning deputy or regent, used for a high office of state in Safavid Iran. The Zand ruler Karim Khan adopted it rather than the title of Shah, presenting himself as regent rather than king.

vakil-al-ruaya.s: Vakil al-Ruaya, meaning Regent of the People, was the title adopted by Karim Khan, founder of the Zand Empire. He refused to take the title of Shah.

vakil-bath.s: The Vakil Bath is a historic public bathhouse in Shiraz, Iran, built under Karim Khan during the Zand period. It forms part of the architectural ensemble with which he adorned his capital.

vakil-bazaar.s: The Vakil Bazaar is the main covered market of Shiraz, Iran, built under Karim Khan during the Zand period. Its vaulted brick arcades formed the commercial heart of the Zand capital.

vakil-mosque.s: The Vakil Mosque is a mosque in Shiraz, Iran, built under Karim Khan during the Zand period, next to the Vakil Bazaar. It is noted for its prayer hall of carved stone columns and its tile decoration.

valencia.s: Valencia is a city on the Mediterranean coast of eastern Spain, surrounded by a fertile irrigated plain known as the huerta. In the medieval period it was an important city of al-Andalus.

valens.s: Valens was Roman emperor in the east from 364 until his death in 378 CE. He allowed Gothic refugees to cross the Danube into the empire, but their mistreatment led to revolt.

valerian.s: Valerian was a Roman emperor of the mid-third century CE who campaigned against the Sasanian Empire. In 260 CE he was captured by the Sasanian king Shapur I after the Battle of Edessa, becoming the first Roman emperor taken prisoner by a foreign enemy.

valladolid-debate.s: The Valladolid debate was a formal dispute held in Spain in 1550–1551 on the treatment of the indigenous peoples of the Americas. Bartolomé de las Casas defended their rights and humanity, while Juan Ginés de Sepúlveda argued that their conquest and subjugation were justified.

valley-of-mexico.s: The Valley of Mexico is a highland basin in central Mexico that once contained a system of shallow lakes, including Lake Texcoco. It was densely populated and home to many city-states.

vandal-conquest-of-north-africa.s: The Vandal conquest of North Africa was the seizure of Roman Africa by the Vandals and Alans between 429 and 439 CE. Crossing from Spain under King Gaiseric, they captured Carthage in 439 and established a kingdom that controlled much of the western Mediterranean.

vandals.s: The Vandals were a Germanic people who migrated through Gaul and Spain before crossing into North Africa in 429 CE. They established a kingdom centred on Carthage and sacked Rome in 455 CE.

vanuatu.s: Vanuatu is an island nation in the south-western Pacific Ocean, formerly known as the New Hebrides. It was governed as an Anglo-French condominium.

varna.s: Varna is the classical Indian system dividing society into four broad orders: Brahmins (priests), Kshatriyas (warriors and rulers), Vaishyas (merchants and farmers) and Shudras (labourers and servants). It was set out in Sanskrit religious and legal texts.

vasco-da-gama.s: Vasco da Gama was a Portuguese navigator who led the first European voyage to reach India by sea, arriving at Calicut in 1498 after rounding the Cape of Good Hope. His voyage opened a direct maritime route between Europe and Asia.

vassal.s: A vassal is a ruler or lord who holds power or land in subordination to a superior, owing loyalty, tribute or military service in return for protection or recognition. Vassalage was a widespread means of extending imperial authority without direct administration.

vassal-and-tributary-systems.s: Vassal and tributary systems describe the recurring pattern by which empires ruled indirectly through subordinate rulers who kept local authority in exchange for tribute, military service and acknowledgement of overlordship. Such systems allowed rapid expansion at low cost but…

vastryoshan.s: The vastryoshan were the commoners in the social hierarchy of the Sasanian Empire, comprising both peasant cultivators and artisans. Society was divided into four estates: priests, warriors, scribes and administrators, and commoners.

venetia.s: Venetia is a historical region of north-eastern Italy centred on Venice. After the Napoleonic Wars it was ruled by the Austrian Empire as part of the Kingdom of Lombardy–Venetia.

venice.s: Venice is a city in north-eastern Italy built on islands in a lagoon, which became a major maritime and commercial republic in the medieval period. Venetian merchants gained extensive trading privileges in the Byzantine Empire from 1082, and Venice played a leading role in the…

verden.s: Verden is a town in Lower Saxony, northern Germany, historically the seat of a prince-bishopric. Under the Peace of Westphalia in 1648, Sweden received the bishoprics of Bremen and Verden, together with Wismar and western Pomerania.

versailles.s: Versailles is a town near Paris and the site of the vast palace built by Louis XIV, which became the seat of the French court and a symbol of absolute monarchy. In 1871 the German Empire was proclaimed in its Hall of Mirrors after the defeat of France.

viceroy-of-india.s: A viceroy is an official who governs a country or province in the name of a monarch. The title is best known for the Viceroy of India, the head of British government in India after 1858, who governed the Raj with the Indian Civil Service.

viceroy-of-kush.s: The Viceroy of Kush, also called the King's Son of Kush, was the official who governed Nubia on behalf of the pharaoh during Egypt's New Kingdom. Accounts of the Egyptian Empire New Kingdom describe the office as a semi-autonomous imperial sub-administration.

viceroy-of-portuguese-india.s: The Viceroy of Portuguese India was the governor of the Estado da Índia, the Portuguese colonial administration in Asia, based at Goa from the early sixteenth century. His authority nominally extended over all Portuguese possessions from East Africa to Japan.

viceroyalty-of-new-spain.s: The Viceroyalty of New Spain was the administrative unit of the Spanish Empire covering Mexico, Central America, the Caribbean, parts of what is now the United States and later the Philippines. It was established in 1535 with its capital at Mexico City.

viceroyalty-of-peru.s: The Viceroyalty of Peru was the administrative unit of the Spanish Empire created in 1542 to govern most of Spanish South America, with its capital at Lima. Its silver mines, especially Potosí, made it a principal source of imperial revenue.

victory-stele-of-naram-sin.s: The Victory Stele of Naram-Sin is a carved stone monument celebrating the Akkadian king Naram-Sin's victory over the Lullubi mountain people, showing the king ascending a mountain above his defeated enemies. It is a masterpiece of Akkadian art.

vienna.s: Vienna is the capital of Austria, on the Danube, and was for centuries the seat of the Habsburg monarchy. It withstood Ottoman sieges in 1529 and 1683, the second of which was broken with the help of a Polish-Lithuanian relief army under Jan III Sobieski.

vienna-secession.s: The Vienna Secession was an art movement founded in 1897 by Gustav Klimt and other artists who broke away from Vienna's established academic art association. It promoted modern styles in painting, architecture and design.

viet-minh.s: The Viet Minh was a Vietnamese independence movement founded in 1941 under the leadership of Ho Chi Minh. It fought against Japanese occupation and then against the restoration of French colonial rule in the First Indochina War.

vietnam.s: Vietnam is a country in mainland Southeast Asia along the eastern coast of the Indochinese peninsula. Its northern part was long under Chinese rule, including periods of Han and Tang administration, and it absorbed Confucian governance traditions.

vijayanagara-empire.s: The Vijayanagara Empire was a powerful Hindu state in southern India founded around 1336, with its capital at Vijayanagara on the Tungabhadra River. It arose as Delhi Sultanate control over the Deccan and the south weakened.

vikings.s: The Vikings were seafaring Scandinavians who raided, traded and settled across Europe from the late eighth to the eleventh centuries. Their raids devastated the coasts and river valleys of the divided Carolingian kingdoms, and accounts of the Carolingian Empire note Charles…

villa-estate.s: A villa, in the Carolingian context, was a great landed estate belonging to the church, the crown or the aristocracy. Accounts of the Carolingian Empire describe these villae as the primary units of agricultural production and local governance.

virginia.s: Virginia is a region on the Atlantic coast of North America, named in honour of Queen Elizabeth I. The colony founded at Jamestown in 1607 was the first permanent English settlement in America.

vishaya.s: A vishaya was an administrative district in the Gupta Empire and other early Indian states. The provinces, or bhuktis, governed by uparikas were subdivided into vishayas.

vishayapati.s: A vishayapati was the official in charge of a vishaya, or district, in the Gupta Empire. Vishayapatis were often drawn from local merchant guilds, working beneath the provincial governors known as uparikas.

vishnugupta.s: Vishnugupta was the last recognised emperor of the Gupta dynasty, ruling around 540–550 CE. By his time the empire had been reduced to a remnant kingdom by Huna invasions, succession disputes and the rise of regional powers.

visigoths.s: The Visigoths were a Gothic Germanic people who entered the Roman Empire in the late fourth century. They destroyed a Roman army and killed Emperor Valens at Adrianople in 378 CE, and under Alaric they sacked Rome in 410 CE.

vizier.s: A vizier is a high minister or chief administrator serving a ruler, a title used in many Islamic states and applied by historians to the chief officials of ancient Egypt. In the Abbasid Caliphate the vizier headed the bureaucracy, and the Seljuk vizier Nizam al-Mulk became the…

vo-nguyen-giap.s: Vo Nguyen Giap was a Vietnamese military commander, the principal general of the Viet Minh and later of North Vietnam. He led the Viet Minh forces in the First Indochina War against France.

volga.s: The Volga is the longest river in Europe, flowing through central Russia to the Caspian Sea. It was a major artery of trade linking the Baltic and northern forests with the Caspian, Central Asia and the Islamic world.

volga-trade-route.s: The Volga trade route was a network of river and portage routes linking Scandinavia and the Baltic with the Caspian Sea and the Islamic world via the Volga River in the early medieval period. Furs, slaves and other goods moved south, while silver dirhams flowed north.

volhynia.s: Volhynia is a historical region in north-western Ukraine. It formed part of the Grand Duchy of Lithuania until 1569.

volta-river.s: The Volta is a river system of West Africa that flows south through present-day Ghana to the Gulf of Guinea. Around 1748, at the height of Oyo power, its tributary network stretched from the Niger River in the east to the Volta corridor in the west.

voorcompagnieen.s: The voorcompagnieën, or pre-companies, were the Dutch trading companies formed in the 1590s to send ships to Asia before the creation of the Dutch East India Company. Their competition drove up prices in Asia and lowered profits in Europe.

viet-cong.s: The Viet Cong, formally the National Liberation Front for South Vietnam, was the communist-led political and military organisation founded in 1960 to overthrow the government of the Republic of Vietnam. Backed by North Vietnam, it waged guerrilla war throughout the Vietnam War…

viking-age.s: The Viking Age is the period from the late 8th to the mid 11th century in which Scandinavians raided, traded and settled across Europe and the North Atlantic. Its beginning is usually dated to the raid on Lindisfarne in 793 and its end to 1066.

vincent-of-saragossa.s: Vincent of Saragossa was a deacon of Zaragoza who was martyred at Valencia in the persecution of Diocletian, around 304. He became one of the most widely venerated saints of Spain.

vir-singh-deo.s: Vir Singh Deo, also written Bir Singh Deo, was the Bundela Rajput ruler of Orchha from 1605 to 1627. In 1602 he had Akbar's minister Abul Fazl killed at the request of Prince Salim, and when Salim became the emperor Jahangir he rewarded him with Orchha and high Mughal rank.

vladimir-ii-monomakh.s: Vladimir Monomakh was Prince of Pereyaslavl and Chernigov and, from 1113, Grand Prince of Kiev. A grandson of Yaroslav the Wise and, through his mother, of the Byzantine emperor Constantine IX Monomachos, he led repeated campaigns against the Cumans and took part in the…

victor-emmanuel-iii.s: Victor Emmanuel III was King of Italy from 1900 to 1946. He appointed Benito Mussolini prime minister in 1922 and accepted the titles Emperor of Ethiopia in 1936 and King of the Albanians in 1939 after Italian conquests.

victor-emmanuel-ii.s: Victor Emmanuel II was King of Sardinia from 1849 and the first King of Italy from 1861. With his prime minister Cavour he allied with France against Austria in 1859, ceding Savoy and Nice to France in 1860, and annexed most of the peninsula.

volunteer-army.s: The Volunteer Army was the main anti-Bolshevik White army in southern Russia during the Russian Civil War, formed in late 1917 by generals Mikhail Alekseyev and Lavr Kornilov and later led by Anton Denikin. Based in the Kuban and North Caucasus, it fought the Red Army and…

vasily-ii-of-moscow.s: Vasily II was grand prince of Moscow from 1425 to 1462. His reign was dominated by a long civil war with his uncle Yuri of Galich and Yuri's sons; in 1446 Dmitry Shemyaka and Ivan of Mozhaysk captured and blinded him.

vasily-iii-of-moscow.s: Vasily III was grand prince of Moscow from 1505 to 1533, son of Ivan III and father of Ivan the Terrible. He completed the gathering of the Russian lands, ending the independence of Pskov in 1510, taking Smolensk from Lithuania in 1514 and annexing Ryazan in 1521.

vere-bird.s: Vere Cornwall Bird was a trade unionist and politician who led Antigua from the 1950s. As chief minister and then premier of the self-governing colony, and from independence in 1981 the first prime minister of Antigua and Barbuda, he dominated politics until 1994, when his son…

victor-amadeus-ii.s: Victor Amadeus II was duke of Savoy from 1675. Changing sides skilfully in the wars of Louis XIV, he gained Sicily and a royal title by the Treaty of Utrecht in 1713, exchanging it for Sardinia in 1720.

viracocha-inca.s: Viracocha Inca was the eighth ruler of the Kingdom of Cusco in Inca tradition. He extended Cusco's power over neighbouring valleys and allied with the Lupaca of Lake Titicaca.

vladimir-lenin.s: Vladimir Lenin was a Russian revolutionary who led the Bolshevik party. He organised the October Revolution of 1917, headed the government of Soviet Russia through the Civil War and founded the Soviet Union in 1922.

vsevolod-the-big-nest.s: Vsevolod III, called the Big Nest for his many sons, was grand prince of Vladimir-Suzdal from 1176 to 1212. He made Vladimir the strongest principality of north-eastern Rus' and dominated Novgorod and Ryazan.

vercingetorix.s: Vercingetorix was a chief of the Arverni who in 52 BCE united most of the Gauls in revolt against Julius Caesar. He used scorched-earth tactics and repulsed Caesar at Gergovia, but was besieged at Alesia, the town of the Mandubii, and surrendered when a relief army failed.

vajrayana.s: Vajrayana, or Tantric Buddhism, is a form of Mahayana Buddhism that developed in India from around the 7th century, using ritual, mantras, mandalas and initiation by a teacher to seek rapid enlightenment. It spread to Tibet, East Asia and maritime South-East Asia, where…

vakpati-munja.s: Vakpati Munja was a king of the Paramara dynasty of Malwa in central India in the late 10th century. A poet and patron of scholars, he raided neighbouring kingdoms, including the Kalachuris, Guhilas and Chahamanas, and fought repeatedly against Tailapa II of the Western…

val-di-chiana.s: The Val di Chiana is a broad valley in eastern Tuscany and western Umbria, running from near Arezzo south to Chiusi and Lake Trasimeno. In Etruscan times its fertile soils supported Clusium, Cortona and Arretium and linked central Etruria with the Tiber and Arno valleys.

valdemar-iv-of-denmark.s: Valdemar IV, known as Valdemar Atterdag, was King of Denmark from 1340 to 1375 and rebuilt the kingdom after years in which its provinces had been pawned to foreign lords, recovering Zealand, Scania and other lands. In 1361 he invaded Gotland and took Visby, provoking war with…

vasyl-chuchupak.s: Vasyl Chuchupak was a Ukrainian insurgent leader who in 1919 organised a peasant self-defence force around the Motronynskyi Monastery in the Kholodny Yar forest of central Ukraine. Declaring loyalty to the Ukrainian People's Republic, the Kholodny Yar Republic controlled some…

via-aemilia.s: The Via Aemilia was a Roman road built in 187 BCE by the consul Marcus Aemilius Lepidus, running in a straight line along the northern edge of the Apennines from Ariminum (Rimini) to Placentia (Piacenza) on the Po. Towns along it, including Bologna, Modena, Reggio and Parma,…

via-francigena.s: The Via Francigena was the main medieval road and pilgrim route from France and northern Europe across the Alps to Rome, described in the itinerary of Archbishop Sigeric of Canterbury around 990. In Tuscany it passed through Lucca, San Gimignano and Siena, whose trade, inns…

vicente-guerrero.s: Vicente Guerrero was a leader of the Mexican War of Independence who kept up guerrilla resistance in the south after 1815. In 1821 he joined the royalist officer Agustín de Iturbide in the Plan of Iguala, which brought independence.

victor-hugues.s: Victor Hugues was a French revolutionary commissioner who in 1794 recaptured Guadeloupe from the British and enforced the National Convention's abolition of slavery there, while executing royalists and sending privateers against enemy shipping. As governor of French Guiana…

vigraharaja-iv.s: Vigraharaja IV was a king of the Chahamanas of Shakambhari in Rajasthan in the mid-12th century who expanded the kingdom north by taking Delhi from the Tomara dynasty, whose chiefs continued as his vassals. A patron of learning, he wrote the Sanskrit play Harakeli Nataka,…

vladislaus-iii-duke-of-bohemia.s: Vladislaus Henry, a Přemyslid prince, was briefly Duke of Bohemia in 1197 as Vladislaus III before giving up the throne to his brother Ottokar I in return for Moravia. As Margrave of Moravia from 1197 until his death in 1222 he united the former Moravian appanages of Brno,…

volodymyr-olgerdovich.s: Volodymyr Olgerdovich was a son of Grand Duke Algirdas of Lithuania who ruled the Principality of Kiev as a Lithuanian prince from about 1362 to 1394. He minted his own coins and kept considerable independence until Vytautas removed him in 1395 and gave him Slutsk and Kapyl in…

vseslav-of-polotsk.s: Vseslav of Polotsk was prince of Polotsk from 1044 to 1101 and a rival of the sons of Yaroslav the Wise. Defeated on the Nemiga river near Minsk in 1067, he was seized during negotiations and imprisoned in Kiev, but the Kievans freed him in 1068 and briefly made him their prince.

vuk-brankovic.s: Vuk Branković was a Serbian noble, son-in-law of Prince Lazar, who after the break-up of the Serbian Empire built up a lordship in Kosovo and northern Macedonia rich in silver mines. He fought at the Battle of Kosovo in 1389 and was later, unjustly, cast in epic poetry as…

valdemar-i-of-denmark.s: Valdemar I, called the Great, was King of Denmark from 1157 to 1182, ending a long period of civil war. With his adviser Bishop Absalon he led repeated campaigns against the Wends of the southern Baltic coast.

vaballathus.s: Vaballathus was the son of Odaenathus and Zenobia of Palmyra, in whose name his mother ruled the Palmyrene Empire after his father's murder in 267. Under Zenobia's regency Palmyra took Egypt and much of Asia Minor, and in 272 Vaballathus was proclaimed Augustus.

vachagan-iii.s: Vachagan III, called the Pious, was king of Caucasian Albania in the late 5th and early 6th centuries, of the Arsacid line. Restored around 485 after a revolt against Sasanian attempts to impose Zoroastrianism, he promoted Christianity, built churches and around 488 summoned…

vaclav-havel.s: Václav Havel was a Czech playwright, dissident and statesman. A founder of the Charter 77 human rights movement, he was imprisoned several times by the communist regime.

vakhtang-vi-of-kartli.s: Vakhtang VI was king of Kartli in eastern Georgia, ruling as regent from 1703 and as king in 1716 and from 1719 to 1724 under Safavid overlordship. A scholar and lawgiver, he compiled a law code, organised the editing of the Georgian chronicles and set up the first printing…

valdemar-ii-of-denmark.s: Valdemar II, called the Victorious, was king of Denmark from 1202 to 1241. He extended Danish power along the southern Baltic and in 1219 led a crusade to northern Estonia, landing at Lindanise, where he built the castle that grew into Tallinn.

valentin-alsina.s: Valentín Alsina was an Argentine lawyer and politician, a leading figure of the State of Buenos Aires after its secession from the Argentine Confederation in 1852. As governor in 1852 and again from 1857 to 1859, he defended the province's control of its port revenues against…

vali-khan.s: Vali Khan was khan of the Kazakh Middle Juz from 1781 until his death in 1819, succeeding his father Ablai Khan. Recognised by both the Russian Empire and the Qing Empire, he struggled to control rival sultans, and Russia began to deal with other claimants, recognising a rival…

valley-of-oaxaca.s: The Valley of Oaxaca is a highland valley in southern Mexico, formed by three arms that meet at the modern city of Oaxaca. It was the heartland of Zapotec civilisation: early villages such as San José Mogote grew there, and around 500 BCE Monte Albán was founded on a hilltop…

vandad-hormozd.s: Vandad Hormozd was a ruler of the Qarinvand dynasty in the Alborz mountains of Tabaristan, northern Iran, in the late 8th century. In the 780s he led a revolt against the Abbasid Caliphate with the Bavandid ruler Sharwin, killing many Arab settlers and officials.

varaz-grigor.s: Varaz Grigor was the first prince of Caucasian Albania from the Mihranid dynasty, a branch of a great Parthian noble family that held the canton of Gardman. Around 630, as the Sasanian Empire fell into crisis, he became ruler of all Albania, governing from Partav, modern…

vasco-fernandes-coutinho.s: Vasco Fernandes Coutinho was a Portuguese nobleman, a veteran of service in India, who received the hereditary captaincy of Espírito Santo in Brazil from King John III in 1534. He landed in 1535 and founded Vila Velha, but attacks by the Goitacá and other peoples, quarrels…

vasco-nunez-de-balboa.s: Vasco Núñez de Balboa was a Spanish conquistador who in 1510 founded Santa María la Antigua del Darién, the first lasting Spanish settlement on the American mainland. In September 1513 he crossed the Isthmus of Panama and became the first European to see the Pacific from the…

vasilko-konstantinovich.s: Vasilko Konstantinovich was prince of Rostov from 1218 to 1238, the eldest son of Konstantin of Rostov. He fought with the forces of Vladimir-Suzdal against the Mongols at the Battle of the Sit River in March 1238 and was captured.

vasily-of-kostroma.s: Vasily of Kostroma was the youngest son of Grand Prince Yaroslav II of Vladimir and the first prince of Kostroma, which he received as his appanage after his father's death in 1246. He fought the Lithuanians and the Novgorodians, and in 1272 became grand prince of Vladimir…

vasily-shemyachich.s: Vasily Shemyachich was prince of Novgorod-Seversky and a grandson of Dmitry Shemyaka. In 1500 he transferred his allegiance and his lands from the Grand Duchy of Lithuania to Moscow, a gain confirmed by the truce of 1503.

vasily-yaroslavich-of-serpukhov.s: Vasily Yaroslavich was prince of Serpukhov and Borovsk, a grandson of Vladimir the Bold and brother-in-law of Grand Prince Vasily II of Moscow. During Moscow's dynastic civil war he loyally supported Vasily II against Dmitry Shemyaka.

vasishthiputra-chamtamula.s: Vasishthiputra Chamtamula, also known as Santamula I, was the founder of the Ikshvaku dynasty in the lower Krishna valley of Andhra in the early 3rd century, after the collapse of the Satavahana dynasty. He built the capital Vijayapuri in the valley now called Nagarjunakonda…

veera-ballala-ii.s: Veera Ballala II was king of the Hoysala Empire in southern India from 1173 to 1220. He declared full independence from the Western Chalukyas around 1187, defeated the Seuna Yadavas and made the Hoysalas the leading power of the southern Deccan, later intervening in the Tamil…

veera-ballala-iii.s: Veera Ballala III was the last major king of the Hoysala Empire, ruling from 1292 to 1343. Malik Kafur, general of Alauddin Khalji, sacked his capital Dwarasamudra in 1311 and forced him to pay tribute.

vela-jimenez.s: Vela Jiménez was count of Álava in the late 9th century, one of the frontier lords of the Kingdom of Asturias. The Asturian chronicles record him defending the castle of Cellorigo against the armies of the Emirate of Córdoba in 882 and 883. Álava was then a largely…

venta-belgarum.s: Venta Belgarum was the Roman town at Winchester in Hampshire, capital of the civitas of the Belgae in Roman Britain. It grew near a late Iron Age enclosure at Oram's Arbour and became one of the larger towns of the province, with a street grid, a forum and defensive walls.

venta-silurum.s: Venta Silurum was the Roman town at Caerwent in south-east Wales, capital of the civitas of the Silures after their conquest in the 70s CE. It had a forum, basilica, temples and baths, and later strong stone walls that still stand.

veronica-gambara.s: Veronica Gambara was an Italian Renaissance poet and stateswoman from Brescia. She married Giberto X, lord of Correggio, in 1509 and after his death in 1518 governed the small state for her sons, defending it during the Italian Wars.

vespasiano-gonzaga.s: Vespasiano Gonzaga was an Italian nobleman, soldier and patron from a cadet branch of the Gonzaga family, who served Philip II of Spain as a military engineer and as viceroy of Navarre and Valencia. From the 1550s he rebuilt his town of Sabbioneta, between Mantua and Parma, as…

vibhaji-ajoji.s: Vibhaji Ajoji was the founder of Rajkot State in the Kathiawar peninsula of western India. A Jadeja Rajput and grandson of Jam Sataji of Nawanagar, he received the area as his share of the family lands and founded the town of Rajkot in 1620.

vibhuti-narayan-singh.s: Vibhuti Narayan Singh was the last ruling Maharaja of Benares, succeeding in 1939 while still a boy. He acceded to the Indian Union after independence, and in 1949 Benares State was merged into Uttar Pradesh.

vibo-valentia.s: Vibo Valentia is a town in Calabria, southern Italy, on the site of Hipponion, a Greek colony founded by Locri Epizephyrii in the 7th century BCE. After a period under the Bruttians, it became the Latin colony of Vibo Valentia in 192 BCE and served as a port on the Tyrrhenian…

victor-paz-estenssoro.s: Víctor Paz Estenssoro was a Bolivian statesman who founded the Revolutionary Nationalist Movement (MNR) and served as president four times. Leading the 1952 revolution, he introduced universal suffrage, nationalised the tin mines and began land reform.

victor-schoelcher.s: Victor Schoelcher was a French politician and journalist who led the campaign to abolish slavery in the French colonies. As under-secretary for the colonies in the provisional government of the Second Republic, he drafted the decree of 27 April 1848 that abolished slavery…

vidkun-quisling.s: Vidkun Quisling was a Norwegian army officer and politician who founded the fascist party Nasjonal Samling in 1933. On 9 April 1940, the day Germany invaded Norway, he proclaimed himself head of government; the Germans soon set him aside, but in 1942 made him…

vieille-montagne.s: Vieille Montagne, in German Altenberg, was a zinc ore mine at Kelmis (La Calamine), between Aachen and Liège, worked since the Middle Ages for calamine used in brass-making. In 1816 the Netherlands and Prussia could not agree who should have it and left the surrounding area as…

vigdis-finnbogadottir.s: Vigdís Finnbogadóttir was president of Iceland from 1980 to 1996, the world's first woman elected head of state in a democratic national election. A teacher and director of the Reykjavík Theatre Company before her election, she was re-elected three times.

vijayabahu-i.s: Vijayabahu I was king of Sri Lanka from 1055 to 1110. Leading resistance from the southern Kingdom of Ruhuna against the Chola Empire, which had ruled northern Sri Lanka since the early 11th century, he drove out the Cholas and took Polonnaruwa in 1070, making it his capital.

vijayabahu-iii-of-dambadeniya.s: Vijayabahu III of Dambadeniya was a Sinhalese king who founded a new royal line after the fall of Polonnaruwa to the invader Kalinga Magha. He established himself at the rock fortress of Dambadeniya in the island's wet zone and recovered the Tooth Relic, making Dambadeniya the…

vijayaditya-iii.s: Vijayaditya III, also called Gunaga Vijayaditya, was the most warlike ruler of the Eastern Chalukyas of Vengi. He fought the Rashtrakutas and their allies across the Deccan, and his inscriptions claim campaigns as far as the Ganges, raising the Vengi kingdom to the peak of its…

vijayaraghava-nayak.s: Vijayaraghava Nayak was the last Nayak ruler of Thanjavur in southern India, a patron of Telugu literature and music at his court. His long reign ended in war with Chokkanatha Nayak of Madurai, whose army took Thanjavur in 1673; Vijayaraghava was killed, and the kingdom soon…

vikramaditya-ii.s: Vikramaditya II was a king of the Chalukyas of Badami in the western Deccan. He defeated the Pallavas and occupied their capital Kanchipuram, where he spared the temples and made gifts to them, and his queens built the Virupaksha and Mallikarjuna temples at Pattadakal to mark…

vikramaditya-vi.s: Vikramaditya VI was the most celebrated ruler of the Western Chalukya Empire of Kalyani. During a fifty-year reign he founded the Chalukya Vikrama era, held off the Cholas and patronised scholars, among them the poet Bilhana, who wrote his biography, and the jurist…

viktor-chernov.s: Viktor Chernov was a founder and leading theorist of the Russian Socialist Revolutionary Party and minister of agriculture in the Provisional Government of 1917. In January 1918 he was elected chairman of the Russian Constituent Assembly, which the Bolsheviks dispersed after a…

viktor-orban.s: Viktor Orbán is a Hungarian politician, a founder of the Fidesz party in 1988 and prime minister from 1998 to 2002 and again from 2010. His government used its two-thirds parliamentary majority to adopt a new constitution, the Fundamental Law of 2011, and his long dominance…

vilmos-tkalecz.s: Vilmos Tkálecz was a Slovene-speaking teacher and politician from the Prekmurje region of Hungary. On 29 May 1919, during the turmoil of the Hungarian Soviet Republic, he proclaimed the independent Republic of Prekmurje, or Mura Republic, at Murska Sobota; it was crushed…

vimara-peres.s: Vímara Peres was a vassal of King Alfonso III of Asturias who took the town of Portucale, modern Porto, from the Moors in 868. He was made count of the land between the Minho and Douro rivers, founding the County of Portugal from which the later kingdom took its name.

vincas-mickevicius-kapsukas.s: Vincas Mickevičius-Kapsukas was a Lithuanian communist leader and writer. He headed the Soviet government of Lithuania in 1918–1919 and then chaired the council of people's commissars of the short-lived Lithuanian–Byelorussian Soviet Socialist Republic, before working for the…

vincent-auriol.s: Vincent Auriol was a French Socialist politician and the first President of the French Fourth Republic, from 1947 to 1954. A former finance minister under Léon Blum, he presided over the Constituent Assembly in 1946 and as president oversaw frequent changes of government in…

vincenzo-i-gonzaga.s: Vincenzo I Gonzaga was Duke of Mantua and of Montferrat from 1587 to 1612. A lavish patron of the arts, he employed Claudio Monteverdi and Peter Paul Rubens at his court, and in Montferrat he built the great citadel of Casale around 1590 to guard the duchy.

virbhadra-singh.s: Virbhadra Singh was the last Raja of the princely state of Bashahr in the western Himalaya and an Indian National Congress politician. After the state merged into India he served six terms as Chief Minister of Himachal Pradesh between 1983 and 2017, as well as a member of…

vishwanatha-nayak.s: Vishwanatha Nayak was the founder of the Madurai Nayak dynasty. Son of the Vijayanagara general Nagama Nayak, he was appointed governor of Madurai by the Vijayanagara Empire around 1529 after a rebellion there, and organised the region into palayams, military fiefs held by…

vistula-lagoon.s: The Vistula Lagoon is a brackish lagoon on the southern Baltic coast, separated from the Gulf of Gdańsk by the Vistula Spit and now divided between Poland and Russia. The Prussian lands of Pogesania and Warmia lay along its shores before the Teutonic conquest of the 13th century.

vladimir-the-bold.s: Vladimir the Bold, Prince of Serpukhov and Borovsk, was a cousin of Grand Prince Dmitry Donskoy of Moscow and his leading general. He commanded the reserve regiment that decided the Battle of Kulikovo against the Golden Horde in 1380, and he defended Moscow during Edigu's raid…

vladimir-the-great.s: Vladimir the Great was Grand Prince of Kiev from about 980 to 1015. In 988 he accepted Christianity from Byzantium and married the emperor's sister Anna, bringing churches, Church Slavonic writing and Byzantine art to Kievan Rus'.

vladimir-yaroslavich-of-galicia.s: Vladimir Yaroslavich was Prince of Galicia, son of Yaroslav Osmomysl. Driven out by his boyars and briefly ousted by Hungary in 1188, he regained Halych with the help of Frederick Barbarossa and Poland.

vladimir-yudovsky.s: Vladimir Yudovsky was a Bolshevik revolutionary in Odessa. In January 1918, after the Bolsheviks took the city, he became head of the council of people's commissars of the Odessa Soviet Republic, which claimed the city and its province until Austro-Hungarian and German troops…

vladislaus-ii-of-bohemia.s: Vladislaus II of Bohemia was Duke of Bohemia from 1140 and its second king from 1158, when Frederick Barbarossa raised him to royal rank for supporting the emperor's Italian campaigns. Barbarossa also granted him the land of Bautzen, beginning Upper Lusatia's long connection…

vladislav-ii-of-serbia.s: Vladislav II was the son of King Stefan Dragutin of Serbia, who ruled the northern lands later called the Kingdom of Syrmia. After Dragutin's death in 1316 his uncle King Stefan Milutin seized most of these lands and imprisoned him; later released, he claimed the Serbian…

vladko-macek.s: Vladko Maček was leader of the Croatian Peasant Party after the assassination of Stjepan Radić in 1928. Through the Cvetković–Maček Agreement of 1939 he secured the autonomous Banovina of Croatia within Yugoslavia and became deputy prime minister; he refused to collaborate…

vojislav-kostunica.s: Vojislav Koštunica is a Serbian lawyer and politician who defeated Slobodan Milošević in the Yugoslav presidential election of September 2000; Milošević's refusal to concede led to the protests of 5 October that overthrew him. Koštunica was President of the Federal Republic of…

volodymyr-shcherbytsky.s: Volodymyr Shcherbytsky was First Secretary of the Communist Party of Ukraine from 1972 to 1989 and a member of the Soviet Politburo. A close ally of Leonid Brezhnev, he replaced Petro Shelest, pursued Russification and repression of dissidents, and led Soviet Ukraine at the…

volodymyr-vynnychenko.s: Volodymyr Vynnychenko was a Ukrainian writer and Social Democratic politician. He headed the General Secretariat, the first government of the Ukrainian People's Republic, in 1917–1918, and in December 1918 led the Directorate with Symon Petliura that overthrew the Hetmanate…

volodymyr-zatonsky.s: Volodymyr Zatonsky was a Ukrainian Bolshevik and member of the People's Secretariat, the Soviet government formed in Kharkiv in December 1917 in opposition to the Ukrainian People's Republic. He later served as people's commissar of education in Soviet Ukraine and was executed…

vsevolod-mstislavich-of-belz.s: Vsevolod Mstislavich was a prince of the Volhynian branch of the Rurikids, a son of Mstislav II of Kiev and brother of Roman Mstislavich. In the later 12th century he ruled Belz as an appanage of Volhynia, making the town the seat of a small principality on the border with…

vukasin-mrnjavcevic.s: Vukašin Mrnjavčević was a Serbian noble crowned king in 1365 as co-ruler with Emperor Uroš V, ruling lands in western Macedonia from Prilep. With his brother Jovan Uglješa, despot of Serres, he led a Christian army against the Ottomans and was killed at the Battle of Maritsa…

vytautas-the-great.s: Vytautas the Great was Grand Duke of Lithuania from 1392 to 1430, son of Kęstutis of Trakai and cousin of Jogaila. He led Lithuanian forces with Poland to victory over the Teutonic Knights at Grunwald in 1410, extended the grand duchy towards the Black Sea, and settled…

vytautas-landsbergis.s: Vytautas Landsbergis is a Lithuanian musicologist and politician who led the Sąjūdis reform movement. As chairman of the Supreme Council he signed the declaration restoring Lithuanian independence on 11 March 1990, the first by a Soviet republic, and led the country through…

val-daran.s: The Val d'Aran is a valley in the central Pyrenees, in Catalonia, Spain, lying on the northern side of the main ridge and drained by the Garonne. Its people speak Aranese, a form of Occitan.

venetic.s: Venetic is an extinct Indo-European language spoken by the ancient Veneti in north-eastern Italy, recorded in some 300 inscriptions from about the 6th to the 1st century BCE. It was written in alphabets derived from Etruscan and shows affinities with Latin and the other Italic…

veneto.s: Veneto is a region of north-eastern Italy, with its capital at Venice, that also includes Padua, Verona, Vicenza and Treviso. It takes its name from the ancient Veneti and the Roman region of Venetia et Histria.

vicenza.s: Vicenza is a city in the Veneto, north-eastern Italy, between the Berici Hills and the Alps. Ancient Vicetia was a town of the Veneti and later a Roman municipium.

vohipeno.s: Vohipeno is a town in south-eastern Madagascar, on the Matitana river near the Indian Ocean coast. It is the historic centre of the Antemoro people, whose ruling clans settled there around 1500 and whose scribal clans kept sorabe manuscripts in Arabic script.

vijayamitra.s: Vijayamitra was a king of the Apracharaja dynasty of Bajaur, the earliest of the line known from inscriptions, ruling in the 1st century BCE. Buddhist reliquary inscriptions are dated by his regnal years; one, the Rukhuna casket, is dated in his 27th year and also in the Azes…

velvet-revolution.s: The Velvet Revolution was the peaceful overthrow of communist rule in Czechoslovakia in November and December 1989. Mass demonstrations began after police beat students in Prague on 17 November, and a general strike forced the Communist Party to give up its monopoly of power.

vahka.s: Vahka, near modern Feke in Adana province of southern Turkey, is a castle in the Taurus mountains north of the Cilician plain. It was an early stronghold of the Rubenid Armenian lords of Cilicia in the late 11th and 12th centuries, guarding routes between the uplands and the…

verica.s: Verica was a king of the Atrebates in southern Britain in the early 1st century CE, the last of the sons of Commius named on coins. His coinage, bearing a vine leaf and the title REX, shows close ties with Rome.

viridovix.s: Viridovix was a chief of the Unelli of the Cotentin peninsula in Gaul who led a coalition against Julius Caesar in 56 BCE, joined by the Eburovices and Lexovii. Caesar's legate Quintus Titurius Sabinus lured the Gallic army into attacking his fortified camp and routed it.

volturno.s: The Volturno is the longest river of southern Italy, about 175 km long, rising in Molise and flowing through Campania to the Tyrrhenian Sea. Ancient Capua and its medieval successor stood near its banks.

vic.s: Vic is a city in central Catalonia, north-eastern Spain, and the capital of the comarca of Osona. It began as Ausa, chief town of the Iberian Ausetani, and keeps a Roman temple uncovered in 1882.

victor-hugo.s: Victor Hugo was a French poet, novelist and dramatist, a leading figure of Romanticism and author of Notre-Dame de Paris and Les Misérables. An opponent of Napoleon III's coup of 1851, he went into exile, living in Jersey from 1852 until his expulsion in 1855 and then in…

visoko.s: Visoko is a town in central Bosnia and Herzegovina on the Bosna river, north-west of Sarajevo. In the Middle Ages its area was the political heart of the Bosnian state: the bans and kings held court nearby, Tvrtko I was crowned at Mile in 1377, and the fortress of Visoki…

vrbas.s: The Vrbas is a river in Bosnia and Herzegovina, more than 200 kilometres long, which rises in the Dinaric Alps, flows north past Jajce and Banja Luka and joins the Sava on the border with Croatia. Its valley was a main route into central Bosnia and was defended by the…

venice-protocol.s: The Venice Protocol was an agreement signed on 13 October 1921 between Austria and Hungary under Italian mediation to settle the dispute over Burgenland. Hungary undertook to withdraw its irregular forces from the region and hand it over to Austria, while a plebiscite was to…

vansda-national-park.s: Vansda National Park is a protected forest in Navsari district of southern Gujarat, India, on the Ambika river near the Western Ghats. Declared a national park in 1979, it covers about 24 square kilometres of former forest of the princely state of Bansda, with moist deciduous…

voortrekkers.s: The Voortrekkers were Dutch-speaking settlers, mainly from the eastern Cape Colony, who left British rule from 1835 onwards in the Great Trek and moved into the interior of southern Africa. They fought the Ndebele and the Zulu, notably at Blood River in 1838, and founded the…

varanasi.s: Varanasi, also called Benares or Kashi, is a city on the Ganges in Uttar Pradesh, northern India, and one of the holiest cities of Hinduism. Pilgrims bathe and cremate the dead at its riverside ghats, and the Kashi Vishwanath temple is dedicated to Shiva.

vareia.s: Vareia was a town of the Berones on the Ebro, at modern Varea on the eastern edge of Logroño in La Rioja, Spain. It was a river port at the head of navigation on the Ebro.

vologases-thracian-priest.s: Vologases was a priest of Dionysus among the Bessi, a Thracian people, who led a major uprising against Roman control in 11 BCE. According to Cassius Dio, his followers killed the Roman client king Rhascyporis and overran much of Thrace.

vadodara.s: Vadodara, formerly Baroda, is a city in Gujarat, western India, on the Vishwamitri river. From the 1720s it was the capital of the Maratha Gaekwad dynasty, whose Baroda State became one of the largest princely states of British India.

vaital-deul.s: The Vaital Deul is an 8th-century Hindu temple in Bhubaneswar, Odisha, India, dedicated to the goddess Chamunda. It is the finest example of the khakhara style, with a barrel-vaulted roof resembling the gopurams of southern India.

venutius.s: Venutius was a leader of the Brigantes of northern Britain and consort of Queen Cartimandua. After their divorce he led the anti-Roman faction against her, and in 69 he drove her out of the kingdom, taking advantage of Rome's civil war.

virgin-gorda.s: Virgin Gorda is the third-largest of the British Virgin Islands, east of Tortola. Its name, the 'fat virgin', is traditionally said to come from Christopher Columbus, who sighted the islands in 1493.

veleda.s: Veleda was a seeress of the Bructeri in Germany in the 1st century CE, described by Tacitus. Living in a tower near the River Lippe, she foretold the success of the Batavian revolt of 69 and was consulted by other peoples, who sent her gifts and captured Roman ships.

vega-real.s: The Vega Real, 'royal plain', is a fertile valley in the north-central Dominican Republic, the eastern part of the Cibao valley drained by the Yuna River. Named by Columbus, it was the land of the Taíno chiefdom of Maguá and the scene of early Spanish gold mining and…

valdivia.s: Valdivia is a city in southern Chile on the Valdivia river, founded by Pedro de Valdivia in 1552. It was destroyed in the Mapuche uprising after Curalaba in 1599 and refounded in 1645 as a fortified Spanish outpost guarding the coast.

verapaz.s: Verapaz is a mountainous region of north-central Guatemala, today divided into the departments of Alta Verapaz and Baja Verapaz. Its Maya peoples resisted Spanish conquest, and the Spanish called it Tezulutlán, the 'land of war'.

vila-velha.s: Vila Velha is a city in the Brazilian state of Espírito Santo, the oldest in the state, founded in 1535 by the donatary Vasco Fernandes Coutinho. Indigenous attacks led the settlers to move the capital to the nearby island of Vitória in 1551, and the first town became the 'old…

vitoria-espirito-santo.s: Vitória is the capital of the Brazilian state of Espírito Santo, built mainly on an island in a bay on the Atlantic coast. It was founded in 1551, when settlers moved there from Vila Velha for safety from indigenous attacks, and became the captaincy's capital.

vila-bela-da-santissima-trindade.s: Vila Bela da Santíssima Trindade is a town on the Guaporé river in Mato Grosso, Brazil, founded in 1752 by Antônio Rolim de Moura as the capital of the new Captaincy of Mato Grosso. Gold mining there relied on enslaved Africans.

valuk.s: Valuk is the first known ruler of the Slavs of Carantania, mentioned in the chronicle of Fredegar as 'duke of the Wends' around 631. He was probably allied with Samo, whose tribal union resisted the Avars and the Franks.

virgil.s: Virgil was a Roman poet of the Augustan age, author of the Eclogues, the Georgics and the Aeneid, the epic of Rome's legendary Trojan origins. The Aeneid became the national poem of Rome and a school text for centuries, and its lines were quoted on coins and inscriptions.

verulamium.s: Verulamium was a Roman town in Britain beside modern St Albans, grown from the Iron Age settlement of Verlamion, a centre of the Catuvellauni. It became a self-governing municipium, was sacked by Boudica's rebels in 60 or 61, and was rebuilt with a forum and theatre.

vedeno.s: Vedeno is a village in the mountains of south-eastern Chechnya, Russia. It became the capital of Imam Shamil's Caucasian Imamate after the loss of Dargo and was taken by Russian forces in April 1859.

vigraharaja-ii.s: Vigraharaja II was a king of the Chahamanas of Shakambhari in Rajasthan in the late 10th century. Breaking free of the declining Gurjara-Pratiharas, he asserted the dynasty's independence, and he is recorded as defeating Mularaja, founder of the Chaulukya kingdom of Gujarat.

vikramaditya-i.s: Vikramaditya I was king of the Chalukyas of Badami from about 655 to 680, son of Pulakeshin II. After the Pallavas had captured Badami in 642 and the kingdom fell into disorder, he expelled them, reunited the Chalukya lands and later raided the Pallava capital Kanchipuram.

virupaksha-temple-pattadakal.s: The Virupaksha Temple at Pattadakal in Karnataka, India, is a Hindu temple dedicated to Shiva, built around 740 by Queen Lokamahadevi to commemorate the victory of her husband, the Chalukya king Vikramaditya II, over the Pallavas. Modelled partly on the Kailasanatha temple at…

vemulawada.s: Vemulawada is a temple town in Telangana, India, near Karimnagar. In the 8th to 10th centuries it was the capital of the Vemulavada Chalukyas, feudatories of the Rashtrakuta dynasty, who patronised the poet Pampa, Jain scholars and Shaiva temples there.

vikramarjuna-vijaya.s: The Vikramarjuna Vijaya, also called the Pampa Bharata, is a Kannada epic by the poet Pampa, completed around 941. A retelling of the Mahabharata centred on Arjuna, it identifies the hero with Pampa's patron, the Vemulavada Chalukya king Arikesari II.

vidyadhara-chandela-dynasty.s: Vidyadhara was king of the Chandela dynasty from about 1003 to 1035, when its power reached its height. He led a coalition that killed the Gurjara-Pratihara king Rajyapala around 1019 for submitting to Mahmud of Ghazni, and resisted Mahmud's later invasions in 1019 and 1022,…

vanga.s: Vanga was an ancient kingdom and region of the Ganges delta in south-eastern Bengal, roughly central and southern Bangladesh. It is named in the Mahabharata and other early texts, and the name Bengal is derived from it.

vikramapura.s: Vikramapura was the capital of several dynasties of eastern Bengal, in what is now Munshiganj district south of Dhaka in Bangladesh. The Chandras, Varmans and Senas ruled from it between the 10th and 13th centuries, and by tradition it was the birthplace of the Buddhist…

vimal-shah.s: Vimal Shah, or Vimala, was a Jain minister and general of the Chaulukya king Bhima I of Gujarat in the 11th century, serving as governor of the Arbuda region around Mount Abu. In 1031 he built the Vimal Vasahi temple at Dilwara on Mount Abu, dedicated to Rishabhanatha, the…

vanraj-chavda.s: Vanraj Chavda, or Vanaraja, was the founder of the Chavda dynasty of Gujarat in the 8th century. According to Jain chronicles written centuries later, he was raised by a Jain monk after his father's death in battle and founded the city of Anahilavada (Patan) around 746, which…

voulet-chanoine-mission.s: The Voulet–Chanoine Mission was a French military expedition of 1899 led by Captains Paul Voulet and Julien Chanoine, sent from French Sudan to conquer the territory towards Lake Chad. Its troops massacred villagers and burned settlements across what is now southern Niger,…

virginia-declaration-of-rights.s: The Virginia Declaration of Rights was adopted by the Virginia Convention on 12 June 1776, drafted mainly by George Mason. It declared that all men are by nature equally free and independent, with inherent rights to life, liberty and property, and protected freedom of the…

via-cassia.s: The Via Cassia was a Roman road running north from Rome through Etruria, past Sutri, Viterbo and Arezzo to Florence and beyond. Built probably in the 2nd century BCE, it remained a main route between Rome and Tuscany in the Middle Ages, when parts of it carried the Via…

viroconium-cornoviorum.s: Viroconium Cornoviorum, at Wroxeter in Shropshire, England, was the capital of the Cornovii in Roman Britain and one of the largest Roman towns in the province. It grew from a legionary fortress of the mid-1st century CE into a civitas capital with a forum and great public baths.

vic-le-comte.s: Vic-le-Comte is a small town in the Puy-de-Dôme department of Auvergne, France, south-east of Clermont-Ferrand. From the 13th century it was the residence of the counts of Auvergne, and its Sainte-Chapelle, built in the early 16th century for the La Tour d'Auvergne family,…

vechte.s: The Vechte is a river about 180 kilometres long that rises in Westphalia, Germany, flows through the former County of Bentheim past Nordhorn and enters the Netherlands, where it is called the Overijsselse Vecht and joins the Zwarte Water near Zwolle. For centuries it carried…

valenciennes.s: Valenciennes is a city in the Nord department of northern France, on the Scheldt near the Belgian border. In the Middle Ages it was one of the two chief towns of the County of Hainaut and a centre of cloth and lace making.

vorarlberg.s: Vorarlberg is the westernmost state of Austria, lying between Lake Constance, the Rhine and the Arlberg pass, with its capital at Bregenz. It was formed from lordships of the counts of Montfort, Werdenberg and Hohenems acquired by the Habsburgs between 1363 and 1765, and was…

villefranche-sur-mer.s: Villefranche-sur-Mer is a coastal town just east of Nice, on one of the deepest natural harbours of the Mediterranean. Founded as a free town by Charles II of Anjou around 1295, it passed to Savoy with Nice in 1388 and became the dukes' main naval base, defended by the Citadel…

vilshofen-an-der-donau.s: Vilshofen an der Donau is a town in the Passau district of Lower Bavaria, where the Vils joins the Danube about 20 km upstream from Passau. Granted town rights in the early 13th century, it passed to the Wittelsbach dukes of Bavaria and lived from river trade.

valls-daneu.s: The Valls d'Àneu are a group of high valleys at the head of the Noguera Pallaresa in the Pallars Sobirà district of the Catalan Pyrenees. In the Middle Ages they formed part of the county of Pallars Sobirà, guarded by the castle of València d'Àneu, and kept their own customary…

vulgrin-i-count-of-angouleme.s: Vulgrin I was a Frankish noble and kinsman of Charles the Bald, who appointed him count of Angoulême and Périgord in 866 to defend the Charente and Dordogne valleys against Viking raiders. He built fortresses at Marcillac and Matha and died in 886.

vaud.s: Vaud is a French-speaking canton of western Switzerland, stretching from Lake Geneva to the Jura with Lausanne as its capital. Long divided between the bishops of Lausanne and the house of Savoy, it was conquered by Bern in 1536 and ruled as a subject territory until the…

vaduz-castle.s: Vaduz Castle stands on a terrace above Vaduz, the capital of Liechtenstein. Built in the Middle Ages and enlarged by the counts of Werdenberg-Sargans and their successors, it was burnt by Swiss troops in 1499 during the Swabian War.

valentinois.s: The Valentinois is a historic district of south-eastern France around Valence, on the left bank of the Rhône. Its counts of the Poitiers family ruled it from the 12th century until 1419, when it passed to the Dauphiné and so to the French crown.

vlissingen.s: Vlissingen (Flushing in English) is a port city on the former island of Walcheren in the Dutch province of Zeeland, at the mouth of the Western Scheldt. Its capture by the Sea Beggars in April 1572 was one of the first successes of the Dutch Revolt.

veere.s: Veere is a small town on the former island of Walcheren in the Dutch province of Zeeland. In the 15th and 16th centuries it prospered as a port under its own lords, and from 1541 it was the Scottish staple, the official market through which Scottish wool, hides and other goods…

valence.s: Valence is a city in south-eastern France, on the left bank of the Rhône, and the capital of the Drôme department. Founded as the Roman colony of Valentia in the territory of the Segovellauni, it became a bishopric and the centre of the Valentinois, held by the counts of the…

vale-of-clwyd.s: The Vale of Clwyd is the broad valley of the River Clwyd in north-east Wales, running from the hills south of Ruthin to the sea at Rhyl. Fertile and sheltered, it is lined by the Clwydian Range with its Iron Age hillforts to the east.

vikrampur.s: Vikrampur is a historic region of central Bangladesh, corresponding largely to modern Munshiganj district south of Dhaka. From the 10th to the 13th century it was the capital of successive Bengali dynasties, the Chandras, Varmans and Senas.

valsad.s: Valsad, formerly Bulsar, is a city on the Arabian Sea coast of southern Gujarat, India, and the headquarters of Valsad district. The district covers the coastal plain and the forested hills of the former princely state of Dharampur.

vucitrn.s: Vučitrn is a town in northern Kosovo, south of Mitrovica in the Sitnica valley. In the late 14th century it was one of the seats of Vuk Branković, and under Ottoman rule it became the centre of a sanjak.

vah.s: The Váh is the longest river in Slovakia, about 400 kilometres long, flowing from the Tatra mountains west and south past Žilina and Trenčín to join the Danube at Komárno. Its valley, guarded by a chain of castles, was the main route through the north-west of medieval Hungary.

vallabhbhai-patel.s: Vallabhbhai Patel, known as Sardar Patel, was an Indian independence leader and the first Deputy Prime Minister and Home Minister of India, from 1947 until his death in 1950. A lawyer from Gujarat, he led peasant campaigns such as the Bardoli Satyagraha of 1928 and became a…

volgograd.s: Volgograd is a city on the west bank of the lower Volga in southern Russia, founded as the fortress of Tsaritsyn in 1589. Its defence against the Whites in 1918–1919, in which Stalin took part, led to its renaming as Stalingrad in 1925.

vardar.s: The Vardar is the longest river of North Macedonia, about 390 kilometres long, flowing from the Šar Mountains past Skopje into Greece, where as the Axios it enters the Aegean near Thessaloniki. Its valley has long been the main route between the central Balkans and the Aegean.

vratislaus-ii-of-bohemia.s: Vratislaus II was Duke of Bohemia from 1061 and the first Bohemian ruler to hold the title of king, granted personally by Emperor Henry IV in 1085 for his support during the Investiture Controversy. He moved his residence to Vyšehrad and founded a chapter there.

vidin.s: Vidin is a port town on the Danube in north-western Bulgaria, built on the site of Roman Bononia. A stronghold of the medieval Bulgarian states, it was from 1356 the capital of the Tsardom of Vidin under Ivan Sratsimir until the Ottomans took it in 1396.

vlachs.s: Vlachs is a historical name, used mainly by outsiders, for the Romance-speaking peoples of south-eastern Europe, ancestors of the Romanians and Aromanians. In the Middle Ages many lived as herders and soldiers across the Balkans and the Carpathians, and they took part in…

veluwe.s: The Veluwe is a forested ridge of sandy hills in the Dutch province of Gelderland, between Arnhem, Apeldoorn and the IJssel. It formed the quarter of the Duchy of Guelders centred on Arnhem.

verviers.s: Verviers is a city in the province of Liège in eastern Belgium, on the Vesdre. Using the soft water of the river, it became a leading centre of wool-cloth making from the 17th century and, around 1800, one of the first places on the European continent to mechanise textile…

vesdre.s: The Vesdre is a river of eastern Belgium, about 70 km long, rising in the High Fens near the German border and joining the Ourthe near Liège. It flows past Eupen, Limbourg and Verviers, and its soft water powered the region's wool-cloth industry.

venlo.s: Venlo is a city in the province of Limburg in the south-eastern Netherlands, on the Meuse close to the German border. A member of the Hanseatic League in the late Middle Ages, it was a fortified river town contested in the wars of the 16th to 18th centuries.

vincenzo-scamozzi.s: Vincenzo Scamozzi was an Italian architect from Vicenza, the leading successor of Andrea Palladio. He completed Palladio's Teatro Olimpico in Vicenza, adding its famous perspective street scenery, designed the Procuratie Nuove on Saint Mark's Square in Venice and built the…

vierlande.s: The Vierlande ("four lands") is a fertile marshland district on the Elbe south-east of Hamburg, named after its four parishes. Pledged by the dukes of Saxe-Lauenburg, it was taken in 1420 by Hamburg and Lübeck, which governed it jointly with Bergedorf until 1868, when it…

vagad.s: Vagad is a hilly, forested region of southern Rajasthan in India, roughly covering the modern districts of Dungarpur and Banswara. It has a large Bhil population and its own dialect, Wagdi.

vanchi.s: Vanchi was the capital of the early Chera kings according to Sangam literature. Its location is debated: most historians identify it with Karur in Tamil Nadu, while others place it near Kodungallur on the Kerala coast.

vijayalaya-chola.s: Vijayalaya Chola was the founder of the imperial Chola dynasty of southern India. A local chief claiming descent from the early Cholas, he captured Thanjavur from the Muttaraiyar chiefs around 848 and made it his capital, at first as a vassal of the Pallavas.

vishnuvardhana.s: Vishnuvardhana was a king of the Hoysala Empire in southern India, ruling from about 1108 to 1152. He defeated the Cholas at Talakad in 1116, freeing Gangavadi, and made the Hoysalas a major power.

volcae.s: The Volcae were a Celtic people known in ancient sources from the 3rd century BCE in southern Gaul, where their two branches, the Arecomici around Nîmes and the Tectosages around Toulouse, held much of Languedoc. Other groups called Volcae lived in central Europe and took part…

volta-redonda.s: Volta Redonda is an industrial city in the state of Rio de Janeiro, Brazil, on the Paraíba do Sul river. It grew around the steelworks of the National Steel Company, founded in 1941 under Getúlio Vargas's Estado Novo with American financing and in production from 1946.

via-salaria.s: The Via Salaria was an ancient road running north-east from Rome through Sabine territory and across the Apennines to the Adriatic coast near Castrum Truentinum. Its name, the salt road, comes from its early use for carrying salt from the Tiber mouth to the Sabines, and it is…

vyborg.s: Vyborg, in Finnish Viipuri, is a port city at the head of the Gulf of Finland on the Karelian Isthmus, now in Russia. It grew around a castle founded by the Swedes in 1293, passed to Russia in 1710 and became part of the Grand Duchy of Finland in 1812.

valentin-gomez-farias.s: Valentín Gómez Farías was a Mexican physician and liberal politician who served as vice-president and acting president several times in the 1830s and 1840s. In 1833–1834, while Santa Anna stayed away from the capital, he launched reforms that ended compulsory church tithes,…

varaguna-ii.s: Varaguna II was a king of the Pandya dynasty of Madurai in the second half of the 9th century. He continued the long wars of the Pandyas against the Pallavas for control of the Kaveri region, but around 885 he was defeated at Sripurambiyam by the Pallava king Aparajita and his…

via-egnatia.s: The Via Egnatia was a Roman road built in the later 2nd century BCE by the proconsul Gnaeus Egnatius after Macedonia became a province. It ran about 1,100 km from Dyrrachium on the Adriatic across the mountains of Illyria and Macedonia to Thessalonica, and was later extended…

verbundbrief.s: The Verbundbrief was the constitution of the city of Cologne adopted in 1396 after the overthrow of the patrician government. It gave political power to 22 corporations called Gaffeln, largely based on the guilds, which elected the city council.

veit-stoss.s: Veit Stoss was a German sculptor and woodcarver of the late Gothic period, active mainly in Nuremberg and Kraków. His masterpiece, the high altar of St.

vechta.s: Vechta is a town in Lower Saxony, Germany, in the Oldenburg Münsterland. Like Cloppenburg it belonged to the Prince-Bishopric of Münster until 1803, when it passed to Oldenburg, and its region remained strongly Catholic.

veraguas-province.s: Veraguas is a province of Panama, the only one with coasts on both the Caribbean and the Pacific, with its capital at Santiago de Veraguas. Its name goes back to the coast Christopher Columbus explored in 1502, and Columbus's heirs held the title Duke of Veragua.

voline.s: Voline, born Vsevolod Mikhailovich Eikhenbaum, was a Russian anarchist writer and activist. After taking part in the 1905 revolution and years of exile, he returned to Russia in 1917 and joined Nestor Makhno's insurgent movement in Ukraine, where he led its cultural and…

vasto.s: Vasto is a coastal town in the province of Chieti in Abruzzo, Italy, on the Adriatic. As Histonium it was a centre of the Frentani and then a Roman municipium.

vetkopers.s: The Vetkopers were one of two rival factions in late medieval Frisia, opposed to the Schieringers. Their feud, which began in the 14th century and was linked to rivalries between chieftain families, monasteries and towns, divided Westergo, Oostergo and neighbouring lands, with…

vlie.s: The Vlie is a tidal channel between the West Frisian islands of Vlieland and Terschelling in the Netherlands, linking the Wadden Sea with the North Sea. In the Middle Ages it was the outlet of waters draining the inland lake that grew into the Zuiderzee, and it marked a…

verritus.s: Verritus was a leader of the Frisii in the mid-1st century CE, named by Tacitus together with Malorix. In 58 CE the two travelled to Rome to ask Nero to let their people keep lands near the Rhine reserved for Roman troops.

victorinus.s: Victorinus was emperor of the breakaway Gallic Empire from 269 to 271. A senior officer under Postumus, he took power after the short reign of Marius and held Gaul and Britain, though Hispania returned to the central empire.

valley-of-elah.s: The Valley of Elah is a valley in the Judaean foothills, the Shephelah, of Israel, running west from the hills of Judah towards the coastal plain. According to the Bible, the Israelites under Saul faced the Philistines there when David killed Goliath.

ventspils.s: Ventspils, German Windau, is a port city at the mouth of the Venta river in western Latvia. A Hanseatic town and later the main shipyard of the Duchy of Courland, it passed to Russia in 1795 and grew after a railway linked it to the Russian interior in 1901.

vidzeme.s: Vidzeme is a historical region of north-eastern Latvia, between the Daugava river and the Estonian border, roughly the Latvian part of historical Livonia. Ruled in turn by German crusader orders and bishops, Poland-Lithuania and Sweden, it passed to Russia in 1721 and formed…

vilnius.s: Vilnius is the capital and largest city of Lithuania, where the Vilnia flows into the Neris. Made the capital of the Grand Duchy of Lithuania by Gediminas in the early fourteenth century, it grew into a centre of Catholic, Orthodox and Jewish life, with a university from 1579,…

vukan-of-raska.s: Vukan was Grand Župan of Raška, the inland Serbian principality, from about 1083 to about 1112. Installed as a governor by King Constantine Bodin of Duklja, he made Raška independent as Duklja declined and from about 1091 raided Byzantine lands around Kosovo and Macedonia,…

vukanovic-dynasty.s: The Vukanović dynasty ruled the Serbian principality of Raška from the late eleventh century until 1166, taking its name from Grand Župan Vukan. Its rulers, based at Ras, shifted between Byzantine and Hungarian alliances and often fought among themselves.

vistula.s: The Vistula is the longest river of Poland, about 1,050 kilometres long, rising in the Silesian Beskids and flowing past Kraków and Warsaw to the Baltic near Gdańsk. Its basin has been the core of the Polish lands since the early Middle Ages and was earlier home to Germanic…

vasai.s: Vasai, formerly Bassein, is a town on the coast north of Mumbai in Maharashtra, India. Ceded by Bahadur Shah of the Gujarat Sultanate to the Portuguese in 1534, it became an important fortified city of Portuguese India until the Marathas captured it in 1739.

veliky-novgorod.s: Veliky Novgorod is one of the oldest cities of Russia, on the Volkhov river near Lake Ilmen. Traditionally first mentioned in 859, it was a centre of the early Rus' and from the 12th century the capital of the Novgorod Republic, a merchant state with a popular assembly, the…

vatsaraja.s: Vatsaraja was a king of the Gurjara-Pratihara dynasty in the late 8th century who made it a major power in northern India. He defeated the Pala king Dharmapala in the Ganges valley but was then beaten by the Rashtrakuta king Dhruva, in the first round of the long tripartite…

vaishnavism.s: Vaishnavism is one of the main traditions of Hinduism, centred on the worship of Vishnu and his avatars, especially Krishna and Rama, as the supreme god. It developed from devotional cults of the late 1st millennium BCE and flourished under many Indian dynasties, inspiring the…

vivarais.s: The Vivarais is a historical region of south-eastern France, west of the Rhône, named after its episcopal city of Viviers and largely corresponding to the modern Ardèche department. It took over the territory of the Gallic Helvii, belonged to the Kingdom of Arles in the Middle…

vibilius.s: Vibilius was a king of the Hermunduri in the 1st century CE, known from the historian Tacitus. In 19 CE he helped to overthrow Catualda, who had ousted Maroboduus as ruler of the Marcomanni, and around 50 CE, together with the Lugii, he brought down Vannius, king of the Quadi,…

veroli.s: Veroli, ancient Verulae, is a hill town of the Hernici in southern Lazio, Italy, above the Sacco valley. With Ferentinum and Aletrium it stayed loyal to Rome in the Hernican revolt of 306 BCE and was allowed to keep its own laws.

vienne.s: Vienne is a city in south-eastern France on the Rhône, south of Lyon. As Vienna it was the chief town of the Allobroges and became a Roman colony, and its temple of Augustus and Livia still stands.

valletta.s: Valletta is the capital of Malta, built on the Sciberras peninsula between two harbours. It was founded in 1566 by Grand Master Jean de Valette after the Ottoman Great Siege, as a fortified city for the Knights Hospitaller, and became their capital in 1571.

vix-note.s: The Vix Note was an Allied demand handed to the Hungarian government on 20 March 1919 by the French lieutenant colonel Fernand Vix. It ordered Hungarian troops to withdraw further west to create a neutral zone, in effect confirming the loss of much of eastern Hungary to Romania.

venta-icenorum.s: Venta Icenorum was the Roman administrative centre of the Iceni, at Caistor St Edmund, south of Norwich in Norfolk, England. It was laid out as a civitas capital after the Boudican revolt of 60-61 and later enclosed by stone walls.

vijayapuri.s: Vijayapuri was the capital of the Ikshvaku dynasty in the lower Krishna valley of Andhra Pradesh, India, in the 3rd and 4th centuries CE. Excavations in the valley of Nagarjunakonda revealed its citadel, palaces, an amphitheatre, bathing ghats and many Buddhist monasteries and…

virapurushadatta.s: Virapurushadatta was a king of the Ikshvaku dynasty of the lower Krishna valley in India in the 3rd century CE, the son of its founder Vasishthiputra Chamtamula. His reign, known from inscriptions at Nagarjunakonda, saw the height of gifts to Buddhist foundations at the…

valentin-vodnik.s: Valentin Vodnik was a Slovene priest, poet and journalist from Carniola. He edited the first Slovene-language newspaper, Lublanske novice, from 1797 to 1800, and wrote the first Slovene poems of the Enlightenment.

volkhov-river.s: The Volkhov is a river in north-western Russia that flows about 224 kilometres north from Lake Ilmen to Lake Ladoga. Novgorod stands on its banks just below the lake, and Staraya Ladoga lies near its mouth.

valka.s: Valka is a town in northern Latvia on the border with Estonia, forming a twin town with the Estonian town of Valga, with which it was one town until 1920. In 1917–1918 it was the seat of the Latvian Bolshevik government, Iskolat, and in 1917 the Latvian Provisional National…

vaidyadeva.s: Vaidyadeva was a minister and general of the Pala king Kumarapala of Bengal in the early 12th century. Sent to put down a revolt in Kamarupa, he took control of the kingdom and then ruled it himself, issuing the Kamauli copper-plate grant as an independent king.

vasudeva-kanva.s: Vasudeva Kanva was a Brahmin minister who founded the Kanva dynasty of Magadha in northern India around 73 BCE. According to the Puranas and the writer Bana, he had his master Devabhuti, the last king of the Shunga dynasty, killed and took the throne.

varna-ratnakara.s: The Varna Ratnakara is a Maithili prose work written by Jyotirishvara Thakur at the Karnat court of Mithila in the early 14th century. It is a manual of descriptions for poets and storytellers, covering cities, courts, seasons, people and crafts.

virgin-lands-campaign.s: The Virgin Lands campaign was a Soviet programme launched by Nikita Khrushchev in 1954 to ease grain shortages by ploughing up unused steppe, mainly in northern Kazakhstan and western Siberia. Hundreds of thousands of volunteers, many of them Russians and Ukrainians, settled…

vagharshapat.s: Vagharshapat is a city in the Armavir province of Armenia, west of Yerevan. Founded or renamed by the Arsacid king Vagharsh I in the 2nd century CE, it became the capital of Armenia after Artaxata, and it is the site of Etchmiadzin Cathedral, seat of the Catholicos of the…

vasavadatta.s: Vasavadatta is a legendary princess of ancient India, daughter of King Chanda Pradyota of Avanti. Stories tell how Udayana, king of Vatsa, was captured by her father, became her music teacher and eloped with her to his capital Kaushambi.

viti-levu.s: Viti Levu is the largest island of Fiji, covering about 10,400 square kilometres and holding most of the country's population. The capital, Suva, lies on its south-east coast and the main international airport at Nadi in the west.

vunivalu-of-bau.s: The Vunivalu of Bau is the paramount chiefly title of Bau in Fiji, originally that of the war king, who shared authority with the senior sacred chief, the Roko Tui Bau. From the 18th century the Vunivalu came to hold real power, and under Tanoa Visawaqa and Seru Epenisa…

vardar-macedonia.s: Vardar Macedonia is the part of the wider region of Macedonia, around the Vardar valley, that Serbia won in the Balkan Wars of 1912–1913 and that belonged to Yugoslavia until 1991. Bulgaria occupied most of it in both world wars, hoping to annex it.

vani.s: Vani is a town in western Georgia and the site of an important ancient settlement of Colchis, on a hill above the Sulori river. Excavations since the 1940s have uncovered temples, walls and rich burials of the 5th and 4th centuries BCE with fine gold jewellery, bronze…

vortiporius.s: Vortiporius was a 6th-century king of Dyfed in south-west Wales, whom Gildas called tyrant of the Demetae and condemned in On the Ruin of Britain. A memorial stone from Castell Dwyran in Carmarthenshire, inscribed in Latin and ogham to Voteporigis the Protector, is often taken…

vale-of-york.s: The Vale of York is a lowland area of northern England between the Pennines and the North York Moors, drained by the Ouse and its tributaries. Its fertile farmland made it the core of Roman, Anglian and Viking settlement around York, and the main road from London to Scotland…

vira-alakeshvara.s: Vira Alakeshvara was the leading figure of the powerful Alagakkonara family in Sri Lanka in the Gampola period. In 1411 the Chinese admiral Zheng He fought his forces, captured him and took him to China, where the Yongle Emperor later released him.

vedas.s: The Vedas are the oldest scriptures of Hinduism, composed in Vedic Sanskrit in north-west India from about 1500 BCE and transmitted orally for centuries. There are four, the Rigveda, Samaveda, Yajurveda and Atharvaveda, each with hymns, ritual texts and later philosophical…

vardzia.s: Vardzia is a cave monastery cut into the cliffs of Erusheti mountain above the Mtkvari river in southern Georgia. Begun under George III and largely built under Queen Tamar in the 1180s, it had hundreds of rooms, a church with royal frescoes and an irrigation system.

vortigern.s: Vortigern was a 5th-century British ruler who, according to Gildas, Bede and the Historia Brittonum, invited Saxon mercenaries under Hengist and Horsa to defend Britain, only for them to rebel and seize land. His historicity and dates are debated.

victory-stela-of-piye.s: The Victory Stela of Piye is a granite stela set up at Jebel Barkal in Nubia by the Kushite king Piye around 727 BCE. Its long hieroglyphic text describes his campaign against Tefnakht of Sais and the rulers of Middle Egypt and the Delta, including the siege of Hermopolis, and…

vienna-awards.s: The Vienna Awards were two arbitrations by Nazi Germany and Fascist Italy that returned territory to Hungary. The First Vienna Award of 2 November 1938 gave Hungary southern Slovakia and part of Carpathian Ruthenia from Czechoslovakia, and the Second Vienna Award of 30 August…

vakhtang-i-of-iberia.s: Vakhtang I Gorgasali was king of Iberia, in eastern Georgia, in the second half of the 5th century. A heroic figure in Georgian tradition, he fought the Sasanian Persians, raised the church of Mtskheta to the rank of a catholicosate and is credited with founding Tbilisi.

vimaladharmasuriya-i.s: Vimaladharmasuriya I was king of Kandy from 1590 to 1604. Brought up as a Catholic by the Portuguese under the name Dom João, he returned to Buddhism, seized the Kandyan throne and in 1594 destroyed a Portuguese army at Danture.

victor-turner.s: Victor Turner was a British cultural anthropologist who studied the Ndembu people of north-western Zambia in the 1950s. His books on Ndembu ritual, including The Forest of Symbols (1967) and The Ritual Process (1969), developed the influential ideas of liminality and communitas.

vanand.s: Vanand was a historical district of Armenia in the province of Ayrarat, centred on the fortress town of Kars in present-day north-eastern Turkey. Under the Bagratids it became the seat of a separate Armenian kingdom, the Kingdom of Kars, created in 963 when Ashot III granted…

varuna-river.s: The Varuna is a tributary of the Ganges in Uttar Pradesh, India, that joins the larger river at the northern edge of Varanasi. The city's name is commonly explained as the land between the Varuna and the Assi, a stream that marks its southern end, and the two rivers frame the…

vidudabha.s: Vidudabha was a king of Kosala in the 5th century BCE, the son of Prasenajit, whom he overthrew. According to Buddhist tradition his mother was the daughter of a Shakya noble by a slave woman, and when he learned that the Shakyas had deceived his father he attacked their…

vili-people.s: The Vili are a Kongo-speaking people of the Atlantic coast of the Republic of the Congo, Gabon and the Cabinda area of Angola. They formed the core population of the Kingdom of Loango, and from the 17th century Vili traders carried ivory, copper, cloth and enslaved people…

velleius-paterculus.s: Velleius Paterculus was a Roman soldier and historian who served under Tiberius in Germany and Pannonia. His short Roman history in two books, dedicated to the consul Marcus Vinicius in 30 CE, is a contemporary source for the reign of Augustus and the early years of Tiberius,…

virunum.s: Virunum was the capital of the Roman province of Noricum, on the Zollfeld plain in Carinthia, Austria. It was founded under Emperor Claudius around 45 CE to replace the hilltop settlement on the Magdalensberg, and had a forum, temples and an amphitheatre.

voccio.s: Voccio was a king of Noricum in the mid-1st century BCE, the only Norican ruler known by name from Roman writers. Julius Caesar records that his sister married the Germanic leader Ariovistus, and that in 49 BCE Voccio sent 300 cavalrymen to support Caesar in the civil war…
