vijayabahu-vi.s: Vijayabahu VI was king of Kotte in Sri Lanka from 1513 to 1521. When he tried to name a younger son as heir, his three elder sons rebelled and had him killed in 1521, an event known as the Vijayaba Kollaya, the 'plunder of Vijayaba'.

vailima.s: Vailima is the estate in the hills above Apia, Samoa, where the Scottish writer Robert Louis Stevenson lived from 1890 until his death in 1894. From there he wrote A Footnote to History (1892) and letters criticising the foreign powers' interference in Samoan affairs.

vijayabahu-kollaya.s: The Vijayabahu Kollaya, the "plunder of Vijayabahu", was a palace revolt in 1521 in the Kingdom of Kotte, Sri Lanka, in which three sons of King Vijayabahu VI killed their father, who had favoured another heir. The kingdom was then divided: Bhuvanaikabahu VII took Kotte,…

virovitica.s: Virovitica is a town in northern Croatia near the Drava river and the Hungarian border, in western Slavonia. A royal free town of medieval Hungary, it was held by the Ottomans from 1552 to 1684 and then became the seat of Virovitica County, which covered much of Slavonia in…

vijaya-champa.s: Vijaya was a region and capital of Champa in present-day Bình Định province, central Vietnam. From around the 11th century it was the chief royal centre of the Cham kings, with the citadel of Đồ Bàn and many brick towers.

vastergotland.s: Västergötland is a historical province in south-western Sweden, between lakes Vänern and Vättern and the Kattegat coast. The core land of the Geats, it had an early bishopric at Skara and its own law, the Västgötalagen.

vastgotalagen.s: The Västgötalagen, or Västgöta Law, is the provincial law of Västergötland in Sweden. Its older version, probably written down in the 1220s and surviving in a manuscript of about 1280, is the oldest Swedish provincial law and the oldest substantial text written in Swedish in…

valsgarde.s: Valsgärde is an archaeological burial site on the Fyris river north of Uppsala in Sweden. Its boat graves, used for generations from about 600 to the 11th century, contained helmets, weapons, horses and feasting gear.

vendel.s: Vendel is a parish in Uppland, Sweden, where rich boat graves excavated from 1881 held helmets, weapons and animal sacrifices. The finds gave their name to the Vendel period of Swedish history, about 550 to 790, just before the Viking Age.

vangio.s: Vangio was a Suebian king of the 1st century CE, nephew of Vannius, the client king installed by Rome north of the Danube. In 50 CE he and his brother Sido, helped by the Hermunduri and Lugii, drove Vannius from power and divided his kingdom between them.

vidovdan-constitution.s: The Vidovdan Constitution was the first constitution of the Kingdom of Serbs, Croats and Slovenes, later Yugoslavia, adopted on 28 June 1921, St Vitus's Day. Passed by a narrow majority while Croat deputies boycotted the assembly, it set up a centralised monarchy governed from…

varangians.s: The Varangians were Scandinavians, mostly from what is now Sweden, who travelled the rivers of eastern Europe from the 9th to the 11th centuries as traders, raiders and mercenaries. They opened the route from the Baltic to Byzantium, and according to the Primary Chronicle…

vima-kadphises.s: Vima Kadphises was a Kushan emperor of the late 1st and early 2nd centuries CE, the son of Vima Takto and father of Kanishka according to the Rabatak inscription. He extended Kushan rule deep into northern India and introduced a large gold coinage, much of it showing the god…

vima-takto.s: Vima Takto was a Kushan emperor of the late 1st century CE, the son of Kujula Kadphises and grandfather of Kanishka. Long known only from anonymous coins issued in the name of Soter Megas, the Great Saviour, he was identified by name when the Rabatak inscription was found in…

vosges.s: The Vosges are a range of low mountains in north-eastern France, running parallel to the Rhine on the western side of the Upper Rhine plain and separating Alsace from Lorraine. Their highest summit, the Grand Ballon, reaches 1,424 m.

volquin.s: Volquin was the second master of the Livonian Brothers of the Sword, from 1209 until his death in 1236. Under his leadership the order conquered the Livs, Latgalians and Estonians, often in rivalry with the bishop of Riga and with Denmark.

valga.s: Valga (Latvian: Valka, German: Walk) is a town on the border between Estonia and Latvia, divided between the two countries since 1920. In the Middle Ages it was a frequent meeting place of the Livonian Landtag, the diet of the Livonian Confederation, whose founding agreement…

valmiera.s: Valmiera (German: Wolmar) is a town on the Gauja river in Vidzeme, northern Latvia. It grew around a castle of the Livonian Order founded in 1283, became a member of the Hanseatic League and was a frequent meeting place of the Livonian Landtag.

villefranche-sur-saone.s: Villefranche-sur-Saône is a town in the Rhône department of eastern France, north of Lyon near the Saône. It was founded around 1140 by the lords of Beaujeu as a 'free town' with privileges to attract settlers, and it became the commercial centre and later the capital of the…

vale-of-glamorgan.s: The Vale of Glamorgan is a fertile lowland region of south Wales between Cardiff and Bridgend, along the Bristol Channel coast. After the Norman conquest of Glamorgan around 1093 its manors were granted to the knights of Robert Fitzhamon, who built castles and churches there,…

vredenburg.s: Vredenburg was a castle built by Emperor Charles V in the city of Utrecht from 1529, after he acquired the secular lordship of the prince-bishops in 1528. Intended to control the citizens, it was besieged and demolished by them in 1577 during the Dutch Revolt.

via-regia.s: The Via Regia, or royal road, was a major medieval trade route across central Europe, running from the Rhineland through Frankfurt, Erfurt and Leipzig to Görlitz, Wrocław and Kraków. Under royal protection, it carried cloth, dyes, salt and other goods for centuries and…

viriathus.s: Viriathus was the leader of the Lusitanians in their war against Rome from about 147 to 139 BCE. A survivor of Servius Sulpicius Galba's massacre of Lusitanians in 150 BCE, he defeated several Roman armies with guerrilla tactics and in 140 BCE forced a treaty recognising him…

vijaya-ranga-chokkanatha.s: Vijaya Ranga Chokkanatha was ruler of the Madurai Nayak kingdom from 1706 until his death in the early 1730s, succeeding the regency of his grandmother Rani Mangammal. His long reign was largely peaceful, but he left government to his ministers and was known mainly for his…

virius-lupus.s: Lucius Virius Lupus was Roman governor of Britain from about 197, appointed by Septimius Severus after the defeat of the usurper Clodius Albinus. With the province's garrison weakened, he bought peace from the Maeatae with large payments, as Cassius Dio reports, and he…

valabhi.s: Valabhi was an ancient city on the Saurashtra peninsula of Gujarat, near modern Vallabhipur, and the capital of the Maitraka dynasty from the late 5th to the 8th century. The Chinese pilgrims Xuanzang and Yijing described it as a rich port and a centre of Buddhist learning…

vikram-samvat.s: Vikram Samvat is a Hindu calendar era that begins in 57 BCE, still widely used in India and the official calendar of Nepal. Tradition links it to a legendary king Vikramaditya of Ujjain, but early inscriptions call it the Krita era or the era of the Malava people.

vorau-abbey.s: Vorau Abbey is a house of Augustinian canons in eastern Styria, Austria, founded in 1163 by Margrave Ottokar III of Styria. Its library preserves the Vorau Manuscript, a 12th-century collection of early Middle High German poetry including the Kaiserchronik.

vermina.s: Vermina was a Numidian prince, son of Syphax, king of the Masaesyli. He commanded troops for Carthage in the Second Punic War and, after his father was captured by the Romans in 203 BCE, ruled what remained of the western Masaesylian kingdom.

vindhya-range.s: The Vindhya Range is a broken chain of hills and plateau scarps across west-central India, running roughly east to west north of the Narmada valley. It has traditionally been seen as the boundary between northern India and the Deccan.

virata.s: Virata is a king of the Matsya kingdom in the Indian epic Mahabharata. The five Pandava brothers and their wife Draupadi spend the thirteenth year of their exile in disguise at his court, and his daughter Uttara marries Arjuna's son Abhimanyu.

volubilis.s: Volubilis is the site of an ancient city near Meknes in Morocco. A Mauretanian town, it became one of the main cities of the Roman province of Mauretania Tingitana, with a forum, a triumphal arch and houses with fine mosaics.

varanda.s: Varanda was one of the five Armenian melikdoms of Karabakh, known as the Khamsa, in the south-east of the region. It was ruled by the Shahnazarian family, whose Melik Shahnazar II allied with Panah Ali Khan in the 1750s and helped him establish the Karabakh Khanate and its…

venus-de-milo.s: The Venus de Milo, or Aphrodite of Milos, is an ancient Greek marble statue of a goddess, usually identified as Aphrodite, found on the island of Melos in 1820. Made in the late second century BCE and probably the work of Alexandros of Antioch, it is about two metres tall and…

vicente-fox.s: Vicente Fox is a Mexican businessman and politician who was president of Mexico from 2000 to 2006. A former Coca-Cola executive and governor of Guanajuato, he won the 2000 election for the conservative National Action Party, ending 71 years of rule by the Institutional…

viminacium.s: Viminacium was a Roman legionary fortress and city on the Danube near modern Kostolac in eastern Serbia, the capital of the province of Moesia Superior. Home of the Seventh Claudian Legion, it grew into one of the largest cities of the Roman Balkans, with an amphitheatre and…

volos.s: Volos is a port city in Thessaly, Greece, at the head of the Pagasetic Gulf below Mount Pelion, and the capital of the Magnesia regional unit. It stands near the sites of ancient Iolkos, Pagasae and Demetrias.

vapheio.s: Vapheio is a site in Laconia, south of Sparta, known for a Mycenaean tholos tomb excavated by Christos Tsountas in 1888. An unplundered pit in the tomb held rich grave goods, above all the two Vapheio Cups, gold cups of about 1500 BCE decorated with scenes of bull-catching.

vitcos.s: Vitcos is an Inca archaeological site in the Vilcabamba region of Cusco, Peru. Manco Inca made it a residence after withdrawing from Cusco in 1537, and he was killed there in 1544 by Spanish refugees he had sheltered.

vanuaaku-pati.s: The Vanua'aku Pati is a political party of Vanuatu, founded in 1971 by Walter Lini and other Anglican-educated leaders and renamed from the New Hebrides National Party in 1977. It campaigned for land rights and independence from the Anglo-French condominium, won the elections…

vryheid.s: Vryheid, Afrikaans for 'freedom', is a town in northern KwaZulu-Natal, South Africa. It was founded in 1884 as the capital of the Nieuwe Republiek, the Boer state set up on land ceded by Dinuzulu.

vsevolod-mstislavich.s: Vsevolod Mstislavich was prince of Novgorod from 1117 to 1136, a grandson of Vladimir Monomakh. In 1136 the citizens of Novgorod arrested and expelled him, accusing him of neglecting the city and fleeing a battle, a turning point after which Novgorod chose its princes by…

vidyapati.s: Vidyapati was a poet and scholar of Mithila in northern Bihar, best known for his love songs in Maithili on Radha and Krishna. He served several kings of the Oiniwar dynasty, notably Shivasimha, and also wrote works in Sanskrit and Avahatta.

vadomarius.s: Vadomarius was an Alemannic king of the Brisigavi in the Breisgau in the mid-fourth century. He made treaties with Constantius II, but in 361 Julian, suspecting him of plotting, had him arrested at a dinner and sent to Spain.

valentinian-iii.s: Valentinian III was Western Roman emperor from 425 to 455, placed on the throne as a child with the support of the Eastern court and ruled at first under the regency of his mother Galla Placidia. His reign saw the loss of Africa to the Vandals and the invasions of Attila,…

vindonissa.s: Vindonissa was a Roman legionary fortress at present-day Windisch, in the canton of Aargau, Switzerland, near the confluence of the Aare and the Reuss. Founded around 15 CE, it housed legions guarding the upper Rhine until about 101, and in the late third and fourth centuries…

valira.s: The Valira is the main river of Andorra, formed at Escaldes-Engordany by the meeting of the Valira d'Orient and the Valira del Nord. As the Gran Valira it flows south past Andorra la Vella and Sant Julià de Lòria into Spain, joining the Segre at La Seu d'Urgell.

vienna-general-hospital.s: The Vienna General Hospital was founded by Emperor Joseph II in 1784 as one of the largest hospitals in Europe, combining care for the sick with teaching. In the nineteenth century it was the centre of the Vienna medical school, where Ignaz Semmelweis discovered the cause of…

vladimir-minorsky.s: Vladimir Minorsky was a Russian-born orientalist and historian of Iran, the Caucasus and Central Asia. After serving as a Russian diplomat in Persia and Turkey he settled in Western Europe and taught at the School of Oriental and African Studies in London.

vorort.s: The Vorort was the leading or presiding canton of the Swiss Confederation before 1848, which convened the federal Diet and conducted common business between sessions. Zürich held the role for most of the time from the fifteenth century to 1798.

vache-ii-of-albania.s: Vache II was a king of Caucasian Albania of the Arsacid line in the mid-fifth century. Forced by the Sasanian king Yazdegerd II to adopt Zoroastrianism, he returned to Christianity and rose against Persia around 459.

vengi.s: Vengi is a historical region of coastal Andhra Pradesh in India, between the deltas of the Krishna and Godavari rivers, named after its old capital near modern Eluru. Conquered by Pulakeshin II around 624, it became the kingdom of the Eastern Chalukyas, who ruled it until the…

vixen-affair.s: The Vixen affair was a diplomatic crisis of 1836 between Britain and Russia. The British schooner Vixen, sent with salt to the Circassian coast to test Russia's claimed blockade, was seized by a Russian warship at Sudzhuk-Kale, near modern Novorossiysk.

vietnam-war.s: The Vietnam War was fought from the mid-1950s to 1975 between communist North Vietnam and the Viet Cong on one side and South Vietnam and the United States on the other, with Australia, New Zealand, South Korea and others sending forces. American combat troops fought from 1965…

vivi.s: Vivi was the first station founded by Henry Morton Stanley in 1879 on the north bank of the lower Congo River, opposite present-day Matadi, as the base for his work for Leopold II. It served as the first capital of the Congo Free State until the administration moved downstream…

vasily-dolgorukov-krymsky.s: Vasily Mikhailovich Dolgorukov was a Russian general who commanded the Second Army in the Russo-Turkish War of 1768–1774. In 1771 he stormed the Perekop lines and occupied the Crimean peninsula, taking Kefe and other Ottoman fortresses, for which Catherine II gave him the…

vaclav-klaus.s: Václav Klaus is a Czech economist and politician who, as finance minister of Czechoslovakia from 1989, led its rapid move to a market economy, including voucher privatisation. He founded the Civic Democratic Party, won the 1992 Czech elections and with Vladimír Mečiar…

vladimir-meciar.s: Vladimír Mečiar is a Slovak politician who led the Movement for a Democratic Slovakia and was prime minister of Slovakia three times between 1990 and 1998. After winning the 1992 elections in Slovakia, he negotiated the dissolution of Czechoslovakia with Václav Klaus.

villers-abbey.s: Villers Abbey is a former Cistercian abbey near Villers-la-Ville in Walloon Brabant, Belgium, founded in 1146 by monks sent from Clairvaux by Bernard of Clairvaux. Richly endowed by the dukes of Brabant, it became one of the largest and most influential monasteries of the duchy.

valentina-visconti.s: Valentina Visconti was a daughter of Gian Galeazzo Visconti, ruler of Milan, who married Louis, duke of Orléans, brother of Charles VI of France, in 1389. Her marriage contract named her as heir to Milan if the male Visconti line failed.

vexin.s: The Vexin is a historical region of northern France between the Seine, the Oise and the Epte. After 911 it was divided along the Epte into the Norman Vexin, part of Normandy, and the French Vexin around Pontoise, held by the French kings.

victor-amadeus-i-duke-of-savoy.n: Victor Amadeus I, Duke of Savoy
victor-amadeus-i-duke-of-savoy.s: Victor Amadeus I was Duke of Savoy from 1630 to 1637, son of Charles Emmanuel I. Married to Christine of France, a daughter of Henry IV, he made peace with France at Cherasco in 1631, gaining part of Montferrat while secretly yielding Pinerolo, and later fought alongside the…

victor-amadeus-iii-of-sardinia.s: Victor Amadeus III was King of Sardinia and Duke of Savoy from 1773 to 1796, succeeding his father Charles Emmanuel III. He reorganised the army and in 1792 joined the coalition against revolutionary France, which promptly occupied Savoy and Nice.

volunteers-of-the-faith.s: The Volunteers of the Faith (Ghuzat al-Jihad) were a corps of North African, mainly Zenata Berber, warriors who served the Nasrid Emirate of Granada from the late thirteenth century. Many were exiled members of the Marinid dynasty and their followers, led by their own…

vega-of-granada.s: The Vega of Granada is the fertile plain around the city of Granada in Andalusia, Spain, watered by the Genil river and its tributaries. Under the Nasrid emirs its dense network of irrigation channels supported cereals, fruit, vegetables and mulberry trees for silk, feeding…

vicente-filisola.s: Vicente Filísola (1789–1850) was an Italian-born soldier in Spanish and then Mexican service. Sent by Agustín de Iturbide to Central America in 1822, he carried out its annexation to the First Mexican Empire and in 1823 took San Salvador, which had resisted.

vladimir-rasate.s: Vladimir-Rasate was ruler of Bulgaria from 889 to 893, the eldest son of Boris I. Soon after his father retired to a monastery, he tried to restore paganism and broke with Byzantium.

valentinian-ii.s: Valentinian II (371–392) was western Roman emperor from 375, proclaimed at the age of four after the death of his father Valentinian I. Dominated by his mother Justina, then by Theodosius I and finally by the Frankish general Arbogast, he never ruled independently.

victual-brothers.s: The Victual Brothers were privateers, later pirates, who first appeared in 1392 supplying besieged Stockholm for Albert of Mecklenburg against Queen Margaret I. They then preyed on Hanseatic shipping in the Baltic and North Sea, occupying Gotland until the Teutonic Order…

valentin-submarine-pens.s: The Valentin submarine pens are a huge concrete bunker at Farge, on the Weser near Bremen, built in 1943–1945 to assemble prefabricated U-boats. Thousands of forced labourers and concentration camp prisoners worked on it, and more than a thousand died.

vegesack.s: Vegesack is a district of Bremen on the Weser, about 20 kilometres downstream from the city centre. Its harbour, built by Bremen in 1619–1623 because silting kept larger ships from reaching the city, is regarded as one of the oldest artificial harbours in Germany.

viet-nam-quoc-dan-dang.s: The Việt Nam Quốc Dân Đảng, or Vietnamese Nationalist Party, was a revolutionary party founded in Hanoi in 1927 by Nguyễn Thái Học and others, modelled on the Chinese Kuomintang. It aimed to overthrow French rule by armed revolt, but the failed Yên Bái mutiny of February 1930…

volta-bani-war.s: The Volta-Bani War was an armed revolt against French colonial rule in 1915–1916 in the region between the Volta and Bani rivers, in present-day western Burkina Faso and Mali. Sparked largely by forced recruitment for the First World War, it united many villages and peoples…

valerius-festus.s: Valerius Festus was a Roman senator who commanded the Third Augustan Legion in Africa in 69–70 CE. During the civil wars of 69 he had the proconsul Lucius Piso killed for Vespasian.

vienna-final-act.s: The Vienna Final Act of 1820 was a supplementary constitution of the German Confederation, agreed at ministerial conferences in Vienna and adopted by the Federal Assembly. It defined the powers of the Diet, set out procedures for federal intervention against disobedient…

vilna-gaon.s: The Vilna Gaon, Elijah ben Solomon Zalman, was a Jewish scholar of Vilnius and one of the most influential authorities on the Talmud and Jewish law. Holding no official post, he studied and taught in seclusion and emphasised rigorous study of texts.

vilnius-university.s: Vilnius University is the oldest university in the Baltic states, founded in 1579 when King Stephen Báthory raised the Jesuit college of Vilnius to the rank of an academy. It became the main centre of learning of the Grand Duchy of Lithuania.

volok-reform.s: The Volok Reform was an agrarian reform of the Grand Duchy of Lithuania introduced by Sigismund II Augustus in 1557. It reorganised royal estates into standard plots of land called voloks, about 21 hectares each, laid out in a three-field system with villages in regular lines.

vytenis.s: Vytenis was grand duke of Lithuania from about 1295 to 1316. He waged long wars against the Teutonic Order, allied with the city of Riga against the Livonian Order and extended Lithuanian influence over Polotsk and Black Ruthenia.

vasily-i-of-moscow.s: Vasily I was grand prince of Moscow from 1389 to 1425, the eldest son of Dmitry Donskoy. With the khan's consent he annexed the principality of Nizhny Novgorod in 1392, married Sophia, daughter of Vytautas of Lithuania, and faced Timur's advance in 1395 and Edigu's siege of…

vasily-kosoy.s: Vasily Kosoy was a son of Yury of Zvenigorod and a contender in the Muscovite civil war of 1425–1453. After his father's death in 1434 he briefly claimed Moscow, but he was defeated by his cousin Vasily II, captured in 1436 and blinded, from which he gained his nickname, 'the…

viva-maria-uprising.s: The Viva Maria was a popular uprising against the French occupation of Tuscany in 1799, which began in Arezzo in May under the cry 'Viva Maria'. Peasant bands led by local notables and clergy drove out the French and their Jacobin supporters and occupied Florence and Siena,…

vocabolario-degli-accademici-della-crusc.s: The Vocabolario degli Accademici della Crusca was the dictionary of the Italian language published in Venice in 1612 by the Accademia della Crusca of Florence. Based on the Florentine of fourteenth-century writers, above all Dante, Petrarch and Boccaccio, it established Tuscan…

verhansung.s: Verhansung was the expulsion of a town from the Hanseatic League, the gravest sanction the Hansa could impose on a disobedient member. An excluded town's merchants lost their trading privileges in the Hanseatic offices abroad.

via-augusta.s: The Via Augusta was the longest Roman road in Hispania, running about 1,500 kilometres from the Pyrenees along the Mediterranean coast through Tarraco and Valentia and then inland to Corduba and Gades. Rebuilt under Augustus, after whom it was named, on the line of older…

veera-ballala-i.s: Veera Ballala I was a ruler of the Hoysala dynasty in southern Karnataka at the start of the 12th century, the eldest son of the prince Ereyanga. He governed as a feudatory of the Western Chalukya Empire and fought neighbouring chiefs to enlarge the family's territory.

vedanta.s: Vedanta is a group of schools of Hindu philosophy based on the Upanishads, the Brahma Sutras and the Bhagavad Gita, concerned with the nature of the ultimate reality, Brahman, and its relation to the self. Its main schools are the non-dualist Advaita of Shankara, the qualified…

vira-someshwara.s: Vira Someshvara was king of the Hoysala dynasty from 1235 to 1263, the son of Narasimha II. He spent much of his reign in the Tamil country, defending the Cholas and building a second capital at Kannanur Kuppam near Srirangam, and divided his kingdom between his sons Narasimha…

viracocha.s: Viracocha was the creator god of the Inca and other Andean peoples, believed to have risen from Lake Titicaca and made the sun, moon, stars and the first humans. The Incas honoured him in Cusco alongside the sun god Inti, and the eighth Inca ruler took his name.

vyatichians.s: The Vyatichians were an East Slavic tribe of the early Middle Ages, living along the upper and middle Oka river, in the area of modern Moscow, Kaluga and Oryol. They paid tribute to the Khazars until Sviatoslav I of Kiev subdued them in the 960s, and Vladimir the Great had to…

vasylko-rostyslavych.s: Vasylko Rostyslavych was prince of Terebovl in Galicia. Immediately after the Council of Liubech in 1097 he was seized by Sviatopolk II of Kiev and David Igorevich of Volhynia and blinded, a crime that broke the princes' agreement and set off a new civil war.

visigothic-code.s: The Visigothic Code, or Liber Iudiciorum, is the law code of the Visigothic kingdom of Hispania, promulgated by King Recceswinth in 654 and revised by Erwig in 681. Unlike earlier codes it applied to Goths and Hispano-Romans alike.

victor-horta.s: Victor Horta was a Belgian architect and one of the founders of Art Nouveau architecture. His Hôtel Tassel in Brussels, completed in 1893, introduced flowing iron and glass forms and open plans into domestic building.

v-weapons.s: The V-weapons were long-range weapons used by Nazi Germany in the last year of the Second World War: the V-1 flying bomb and the V-2 ballistic missile, the first of its kind. From June 1944 they were launched against London and, after its liberation, against the port of…

visegrad.s: Visegrád is a small town in northern Hungary on the bend of the Danube. In the fourteenth century Charles I made it the royal seat, and in 1335 the kings of Hungary, Bohemia and Poland met there to settle disputes and agree on trade.

vltava.s: The Vltava is the longest river of the Czech Republic, rising in the Bohemian Forest and flowing north through České Budějovice and Prague to join the Elbe at Mělník. Its basin forms the heart of Bohemia, and Prague grew around its crossing points.

ven-island.s: Ven is a small island in the Øresund between Zealand and Scania, part of Sweden since the Treaty of Roskilde of 1658. In 1576 King Frederick II of Denmark granted it to the astronomer Tycho Brahe, who built the observatories of Uraniborg and Stjerneborg there and made precise…

vata-pagan-uprising.s: The Vata pagan uprising was a revolt in Hungary in 1046, led by a nobleman named Vata, against Christianity and the rule of King Peter Orseolo. The rebels killed Bishop Gerard of Csanád and other clergy and overthrew Peter, but Andrew I, whom they helped to the throne,…

visegrad-group.s: The Visegrád Group is a regional alliance of Czechia, Hungary, Poland and Slovakia, founded at Visegrád in Hungary in February 1991 by Czechoslovakia, Hungary and Poland. Its name recalls the meeting of the kings of Hungary, Bohemia and Poland at Visegrád in 1335.

veluvana.s: Veluvana, the Bamboo Grove, was a park outside Rajagriha, the capital of Magadha, which King Bimbisara gave to the Buddha and his order of monks. It is remembered as the first monastery donated to the Buddhist sangha, and the Buddha spent several rainy seasons there.

victoria-and-albert-museum.s: The Victoria and Albert Museum in London is the world's largest museum of decorative arts and design, founded in 1852 after the Great Exhibition and given its present name in 1899 after Queen Victoria and Prince Albert. Its collections span ceramics, textiles, furniture,…

via-toledo.s: Via Toledo is one of the main streets of Naples, laid out in 1536 by the Spanish viceroy Pedro de Toledo along the line of the old western walls. Running for over a kilometre from Piazza Dante towards the royal palace, it became the city's principal thoroughfare, lined with…

varangian-guard.s: The Varangian Guard was the elite bodyguard of the Byzantine emperors, formed around 988 when Basil II received about 6,000 warriors from Vladimir of Kiev. At first made up of Rus' and Scandinavians, among them the future king Harald Hardrada, it later recruited many…

valle-crucis-abbey.s: Valle Crucis Abbey is a ruined Cistercian abbey near Llangollen in north-east Wales, founded in 1201 by Madog ap Gruffudd Maelor, prince of northern Powys. Its name, 'valley of the cross', comes from the nearby Pillar of Eliseg.

victor-emmanuel-i-of-sardinia.s: Victor Emmanuel I was King of Sardinia from 1802 to 1821. While the French held Piedmont he lived on the island of Sardinia, and in 1814 he returned to Turin, where he restored the old order and in 1815 gained the former Republic of Genoa.

vita-karoli-magni.s: The Vita Karoli Magni, or Life of Charlemagne, is a biography of the Frankish emperor written by his courtier Einhard, probably in the 820s. Modelled on Suetonius' lives of the Roman emperors, it describes Charlemagne's wars, character, family and habits.

vincent-van-gogh.s: Vincent van Gogh was a Dutch Post-Impressionist painter whose expressive colour and brushwork made him one of the most influential artists of modern times. He painted most of his works, among them The Potato Eaters, Sunflowers and The Starry Night, in about a decade, much of…

van-fortress.s: Van Fortress, or Van Kalesi, is a massive citadel on a long limestone ridge on the eastern shore of Lake Van in eastern Turkey. It was the site of Tushpa, the capital of Urartu from the ninth century BCE, and preserves rock-cut tombs and inscriptions, including the annals of…

vasudeva-i.s: Vasudeva I was the last great emperor of the Kushan Empire, whose inscriptions date roughly from 190 to 230 CE and are concentrated around Mathura. He was the first Kushan ruler to bear a purely Indian name, and his coins favour the god Shiva.

vasishka.s: Vasishka was a Kushan emperor of the 3rd century CE, one of the successors of Vasudeva I during the empire's decline. He is known from inscriptions dated in the Kanishka era and from coins, and ruled a reduced realm in north-western India while the Sasanians advanced in Bactria.

vasudeva-ii.s: Vasudeva II was one of the last Kushan kings, ruling in the later 3rd century CE over a much reduced realm around the Indus and the Punjab. He is known mainly from coins, which grew increasingly debased.

visoun.s: Visoun was king of Lan Xang from 1500 to 1520. He brought the Phra Bang, the revered Buddha image, to the capital, which was later renamed Luang Prabang after it, and founded Wat Visoun there.

vietnamese-alphabet.s: The Vietnamese alphabet, chữ Quốc ngữ, is the Latin-based script used to write Vietnamese, with diacritics marking tones and vowels. Developed by Portuguese and French Catholic missionaries in the 17th century, notably Alexandre de Rhodes, it was promoted under French rule and…

vipasca.s: Vipasca was a Roman mining settlement in Lusitania, at modern Aljustrel in southern Portugal, where copper and silver were extracted. Two bronze tablets found there preserve imperial regulations, probably of Hadrian's reign, for the leasing and working of the mines and for the…

vijaydurg.s: Vijaydurg is a sea fort on the Konkan coast of Maharashtra, India, at the mouth of the Waghotan river. Strengthened by Shivaji in the 17th century, it became a main base of the Maratha navy under Kanhoji Angre and his successors and repelled attacks by the English East India…

vitkovice-ironworks.s: The Vítkovice ironworks in Ostrava were founded in 1828 by Archduke Rudolf, archbishop of Olomouc, and were later owned by the Rothschild family. Using coal from the Ostrava basin, they became one of the largest iron and steel works in the Habsburg Monarchy and the core of…

vladislaus-ii-of-hungary.s: Vladislaus II of Hungary, of the Jagiellonian dynasty, was elected King of Bohemia in 1471 and King of Hungary in 1490. Weak in both kingdoms, he left power to the estates and magnates, and the Vladislav Land Ordinance of 1500 confirmed noble dominance in Bohemia.

vazimba.s: The Vazimba are, in Malagasy tradition, the earliest inhabitants of the central highlands of Madagascar, displaced or absorbed by the ancestors of the Merina. Royal traditions credit King Andriamanelo with defeating them with iron-tipped spears in the sixteenth century.

venustiano-carranza.s: Venustiano Carranza was a Mexican politician who led the Constitutionalist movement against Victoriano Huerta from 1913 and was president from 1917 to 1920. He convened the congress at Querétaro that drafted the Constitution of 1917.

victoriano-huerta.s: Victoriano Huerta was a Mexican general who seized power in February 1913 in a coup against President Francisco Madero, who was then murdered. His dictatorship faced the Constitutionalist rebellion and the hostility of the United States, which occupied Veracruz in 1914.

volksgemeinschaft.s: Volksgemeinschaft, or 'people's community', was the Nazi ideal of a united German nation standing above class, religion and party. In Nazi ideology it was defined by race, excluding Jews and others deemed alien or unfit, and it was promoted through mass organisations, rallies,…

valenciana-mine.s: The Valenciana mine was a silver mine at Guanajuato in central Mexico, opened by Antonio de Obregón y Alcocer in the 1760s. By the end of the eighteenth century it was the richest silver mine in the world, producing a large share of New Spain's output, and its owners became…

vinh-te-canal.s: The Vĩnh Tế Canal is a canal of about 90 kilometres in the Mekong delta, running along the Cambodian border from Châu Đốc to Hà Tiên on the Gulf of Thailand. Dug between 1819 and 1824 under Gia Long and Minh Mạng by tens of thousands of Vietnamese and Khmer labourers, it…

villmergen-wars.s: The Villmergen Wars were two religious civil wars of the Old Swiss Confederacy, both named after battles fought at Villmergen in the Aargau. In the first, in 1656, the Catholic cantons defeated Zürich and Bern; in the second, in 1712, also called the Toggenburg War, the…

varendra-rebellion.s: The Varendra rebellion was a revolt of the Kaivartas, a community of boatmen and cultivators, against the Pala dynasty in northern Bengal in the late eleventh century. Under their leader Divya the rebels killed King Mahipala II and held Varendra, the Pala homeland, for a…

varendra.s: Varendra is a historical region of northern Bengal between the Ganges and the Karatoya rivers, largely within the present Rajshahi Division of Bangladesh and the adjoining districts of West Bengal. It was the ancestral homeland of the Pala dynasty, lost to the Kaivarta rebels…

vaikuntha-perumal-temple.s: The Vaikuntha Perumal Temple is a Hindu temple to Vishnu in Kanchipuram, Tamil Nadu, built by the Pallava king Nandivarman II in the eighth century. Its sanctuary has three storeys, each with an image of Vishnu, and the sculptured panels of its cloister are thought to show…

vatican-library.s: The Vatican Library is the library of the Holy See in Vatican City, formally established in 1475 by Pope Sixtus IV, building on the collection of Nicholas V. It holds one of the world's most important collections of manuscripts, including the Codex Vaticanus of the Bible.

vologases-vi.s: Vologases VI was a king of the Parthian Empire who reigned from about 208 to 228 CE. He spent most of his reign disputing the throne with his brother Artabanus IV, who controlled much of the empire, while Vologases held Mesopotamia and issued coins at Seleucia.

venice-commission.s: The Venice Commission, formally the European Commission for Democracy through Law, is an advisory body of the Council of Europe founded in 1990. Made up of independent experts in constitutional law, it gives opinions on constitutions and laws of member states; in 2002 it…

vasile-lupu.s: Vasile Lupu was Prince of Moldavia from 1634 to 1653, a wealthy ruler of Albanian descent whose long reign brought relative prosperity. He built the Church of the Three Hierarchs in Iași, set up a printing press, and issued the law code Carte românească de învățătură (1646).

vijayaditya-ii.s: Vijayaditya II, also called Narendra Mrigaraja, was a king of the Eastern Chalukya dynasty of Vengi in the first half of the ninth century. He fought a long series of battles against the Rashtrakutas and their allies over control of Vengi, and Rashtrakuta records claim that…

vajiravudh.s: Vajiravudh, Rama VI, was king of Siam from 1910 to 1925, educated at Sandhurst and Oxford. He promoted a royalist Thai nationalism, founded the Wild Tiger Corps, introduced surnames and compulsory primary education, and founded Chulalongkorn University.

valparaiso.s: Valparaíso is a port city in central Chile, built on steep hills above a bay on the Pacific. Founded by the Spanish in 1536, it became the main commercial port of the South American Pacific in the nineteenth century, before the opening of the Panama Canal.

vaps-movement.s: The Vaps Movement, formally the Estonian War of Independence Veterans' League, was a radical right-wing populist movement of the early 1930s. It campaigned against parliamentary government and drafted the constitution approved by referendum in 1933, which created a powerful…

vicente-cerna-y-cerna.s: Vicente Cerna y Cerna (1815–1885) was a Guatemalan general and conservative politician who succeeded Rafael Carrera as president in 1865. He continued Carrera's alliance with the church and the conservative elite but faced growing liberal opposition, and he was overthrown in…

vinicio-cerezo.s: Vinicio Cerezo (born 1942) is a Guatemalan Christian Democrat politician who was president from 1986 to 1991, the first civilian elected under the constitution of 1985 after decades of military rule. He hosted the Esquipulas summits that produced the Central American peace…

vaira-vike-freiberga.s: Vaira Vīķe-Freiberga is a Latvian-Canadian psychologist and politician who was president of Latvia from 1999 to 2007, the first woman to hold the office. Born in Riga, she fled with her family in 1944 and built an academic career at the University of Montreal before returning…

vef.s: VEF (Valsts Elektrotehniskā Fabrika, State Electrotechnical Factory) was a state-owned electrical manufacturer in Riga, established in 1919. In the 1930s it became known for radios, telephones, light aircraft and, from 1938, the Minox miniature camera.

valdas-adamkus.s: Valdas Adamkus is a Lithuanian-American environmental official and politician who was president of Lithuania from 1998 to 2003 and from 2004 to 2009. Having emigrated to the United States after the Second World War, he worked for the US Environmental Protection Agency before…

vytautas-magnus-university.s: Vytautas Magnus University is a university in Kaunas, founded in 1922 as the University of Lithuania and renamed in 1930 after the medieval grand duke Vytautas the Great. As the main university of interwar Lithuania it trained the national elite while Vilnius was under Polish…

violeta-chamorro.s: Violeta Barrios de Chamorro was a Nicaraguan publisher and politician who was president of Nicaragua from 1990 to 1997, the first woman elected president in the Americas. The widow of Pedro Joaquín Chamorro, she briefly sat on the Sandinista junta in 1979–1980 before leading…

victor-raul-haya-de-la-torre.n: Víctor Raúl Haya de la Torre
victor-raul-haya-de-la-torre.s: Víctor Raúl Haya de la Torre was a Peruvian political leader who founded APRA in 1924 as a continental anti-imperialist movement and led it for more than half a century. Repeatedly imprisoned or exiled, and barred by the army from taking power, he spent five years in asylum in…

vladimiro-montesinos.s: Vladimiro Montesinos was the de facto head of Peru's National Intelligence Service and the most powerful adviser of President Alberto Fujimori in the 1990s. In September 2000 a video showing him bribing an opposition congressman was broadcast, causing the collapse of…

venetian-dalmatia.s: Venetian Dalmatia was the Republic of Venice's possession on the eastern Adriatic coast, held from 1420, when Venice bought the Hungarian claim and took over most coastal towns, until the fall of the republic in 1797. Governed from Zadar, it supplied sailors, timber and soldiers.

vaal-triangle.s: The Vaal Triangle is an industrial region on the Vaal River south of Johannesburg, formed by the towns of Vereeniging, Vanderbijlpark and Sasolburg and their townships, among them Sharpeville and Sebokeng. Its steel and chemical works made it an industrial heartland.

victor-lieberman.s: Victor Lieberman is an American historian of South-East Asia at the University of Michigan. His Burmese Administrative Cycles (1984) studied the Toungoo state, and his two-volume Strange Parallels (2003–2009) compared state formation in mainland South-East Asia with that of…

vladimir-mayakovsky.s: Vladimir Mayakovsky was a Russian poet, playwright and artist and a leading figure of Russian Futurism. He welcomed the 1917 revolution and put his bold, declamatory verse and his posters at its service, in works such as the poem 150,000,000 and the play The Bedbug.

volga-germans.s: The Volga Germans were ethnic Germans who settled along the lower Volga in Russia from the 1760s, invited by Catherine the Great with promises of land and religious freedom. In 1924 they received an autonomous Soviet republic.

vasishthiputra-pulumavi.s: Vasishthiputra Pulumavi was a Satavahana king of the Deccan in the second century CE, son and successor of Gautamiputra Satakarni. Under him the kingdom extended from the western coast to the Krishna delta, and his inscriptions appear at Nashik, Karle and Amaravati.

vietnamese-fatherland-front.s: The Vietnamese Fatherland Front is the umbrella organisation, led by the Communist Party, that groups Vietnam's officially recognised mass organisations, such as the trade unions, the women's union and the youth union. Founded in North Vietnam in 1955, it absorbed the southern…

vi-xuyen.s: Vị Xuyên is a mountainous area of Hà Giang in the far north of Vietnam, on the border with China's Yunnan province, long administered as a district. From 1984 to 1989 it was the main battlefield of the Sino-Vietnamese border conflict that followed the war of 1979, with…

virarajendra-chola.s: Virarajendra Chola was a king of the Chola dynasty of south India, ruling from 1063 to 1070, a son of Rajendra Chola I. He fought repeated wars against the Western Chalukyas, defeating them at Kudal Sangamam, and campaigned in Sri Lanka.

visayas.s: The Visayas are the central group of islands of the Philippines, between Luzon and Mindanao, including Panay, Negros, Cebu, Bohol, Leyte and Samar. Colonised by Spain from the 1560s, their coastal settlements suffered raids by fleets from the Sulu zone for more than two…

voltaire.s: Voltaire, the pen name of François-Marie Arouet, was a French writer and philosopher and the most famous figure of the Enlightenment. In plays, histories, satires such as Candide and polemics he attacked religious intolerance, the power of the Church and arbitrary government.

vasili-iv-of-russia.s: Vasili IV Shuisky was tsar of Russia from 1606 to 1610, during the Time of Troubles. A leading boyar of a Rurikid princely family, he took the throne after the murder of the first False Dmitry but faced the Bolotnikov rebellion and a second pretender.

vijay-stambha.s: The Vijay Stambha, or Tower of Victory, is a nine-storey tower in Chittor Fort built by Rana Kumbha of Mewar in the mid-fifteenth century to commemorate his victory over Mahmud Khalji of Malwa. Rising about 37 metres and dedicated to Vishnu, it is covered inside and out with…

voting-rights-act-of-1965.s: The Voting Rights Act of 1965 is a United States law, signed by President Lyndon B. Johnson in August 1965 after the Selma to Montgomery marches, that prohibited racial discrimination in voting.

viernes-negro.s: Viernes Negro, or Black Friday, was 18 February 1983, when the Venezuelan government of Luis Herrera Campins devalued the bolívar and introduced exchange controls after falling oil prices and heavy foreign debt had drained the reserves. It ended two decades of a stable, strong…

vellore.s: Vellore is a city in the north of Tamil Nadu, India, known for its sixteenth-century fort built under the Vijayanagara Empire. In the empire's final decades it served, with Chandragiri, as a royal seat of the Aravidu kings.

venkatapati-raya.s: Venkatapati Raya, or Venkata II, was emperor of Vijayanagara of the Aravidu dynasty from 1586 to 1614. Ruling from Penukonda and later Chandragiri, he restored a measure of royal authority, repelled attacks by Golconda and kept the southern nayakas in nominal obedience.

vidyaranya.s: Vidyaranya was a fourteenth-century Hindu scholar and ascetic who became head of the Sringeri monastery founded by Adi Shankara. Later tradition credits him with guiding Harihara I and Bukka I in founding the Vijayanagara Empire, though many historians doubt the story.

vittala-temple.s: The Vittala Temple is a Hindu temple at Hampi in Karnataka, dedicated to Vitthala, a form of Vishnu, and built mainly in the fifteenth and sixteenth centuries under the Vijayanagara Empire, with additions in the reign of Krishnadevaraya. It is famous for its stone chariot and…

volga-tatars.s: The Volga Tatars are a Turkic people of the middle Volga and Ural regions of Russia, most of whom live in Tatarstan and neighbouring republics; they are the largest group of Tatars and are mainly Sunni Muslims. Their language belongs to the Kipchak branch of Turkic.

veliky-ustyug.s: Veliky Ustyug is a town in Vologda Oblast in northern Russia, at the confluence of the Sukhona and Yug rivers, first mentioned in the chronicles in 1207. A frontier outpost of Rostov and Vladimir-Suzdal on the route to the northern fur lands, it was captured by the Volga…

vikramankadevacharita.s: The Vikramankadevacharita is a Sanskrit poem in eighteen cantos by the Kashmiri poet Bilhana, written in the 1080s, celebrating the life of his patron, the Western Chalukya king Vikramaditya VI. Part history and part court epic, it describes the king's rise to the throne and…

vikramashila.s: Vikramashila was a great Buddhist monastery and centre of learning in the Bhagalpur district of Bihar, India, founded by the Pala emperor Dharmapala around 800. With Nalanda it was one of the leading universities of Buddhist India, specialising in tantric Buddhism, and its…

vishnugopa-of-kanchi.s: Vishnugopa of Kanchi was a Pallava king of Kanchipuram in the mid-4th century. He is named in the Allahabad pillar inscription of the Gupta emperor Samudragupta among the southern kings who were defeated and then reinstated during Samudragupta's southern campaign, which makes…

vendome-column.s: The Vendôme Column is a monumental column in the Place Vendôme in Paris, erected in 1806–1810 on Napoleon's orders to commemorate the victory at Austerlitz. Modelled on Trajan's Column, it is sheathed in bronze reliefs said to be cast from captured enemy cannon and topped by a…

vale-of-pickering.s: The Vale of Pickering is a low-lying plain in North Yorkshire, England, between the North York Moors and the Yorkshire Wolds, drained by the River Derwent. At the end of the last Ice Age it held a glacial lake, and its former wetlands preserve major prehistoric sites, among…

vardan-mamikonian.s: Vardan Mamikonian was an Armenian military leader of the Mamikonian noble house who led the Christian rising against the Sasanian king Yazdegerd II's attempt to impose Zoroastrianism. He was killed at the Battle of Avarayr in 451, but the resistance he began eventually secured…

vaal-river.s: The Vaal River is the largest tributary of the Orange River in South Africa, flowing about 1,120 kilometres westwards from Mpumalanga. In the 19th century it marked the boundary between the Orange Free State to the south and the South African Republic, the Transvaal, which…

vic-sur-seille.s: Vic-sur-Seille is a small town in Lorraine, north-eastern France. Its salt works enriched the bishops of Metz, who made it their residence after the citizens of Metz won independence in the 13th century.

valais.s: Valais is a canton in south-western Switzerland covering the upper valley of the Rhône, with Sion as its capital. Ruled by the bishops of Sion from 999, it saw the communes of the German-speaking upper valley take power and conquer the French-speaking lower valley from Savoy…

verdun.s: Verdun is a town on the Meuse in north-eastern France, the seat of a bishop since late Roman times. The treaty that divided the Carolingian Empire was signed there in 843, and its bishops later ruled a principality of the Holy Roman Empire.

vinschgau.s: The Vinschgau (Italian Val Venosta) is the valley of the upper Adige in South Tyrol, northern Italy, running from the Reschen Pass down to Merano. A route between the Alpine passes and Italy since Roman times, it was disputed in the Middle Ages between the bishops of Chur and…

veps.s: The Veps are a small Finnic people of north-western Russia, living between Lakes Ladoga, Onega and Beloye. They are usually identified with the Ves named in the Russian Primary Chronicle among the peoples of the north who invited Rurik and his brothers.

volodar-rostyslavych.s: Volodar Rostyslavych was a Rurikid prince of Peremyshl, now Przemyśl, in south-western Rus'. With his brothers Rurik and Vasylko he took control of the towns of the region in the 1080s and defended them against Kiev, Poland and Hungary.

volodymyrko-volodarovych.s: Volodymyrko Volodarovych was a prince of Zvenyhorod and Peremyshl who united the lands of his family and in 1141 made Halych on the Dniester their capital, creating the Principality of Galicia. He defended its independence against Kiev and Hungary through shifting alliances.

vogelsberg.s: The Vogelsberg is a range of low mountains in central Hesse, Germany, the eroded remains of a large Miocene volcano and one of the biggest basalt areas in Central Europe. Its highest point, the Taufstein, rises to 773 metres.

visvaldis.s: Visvaldis, called Vissewalde in German sources, was the prince of Jersika on the Daugava in present-day Latvia in the early 13th century. Of mixed Latgalian and Rus' background and a vassal of Polotsk, he resisted the Livonian crusaders, but after Bishop Albert of Riga sacked…

vakhsh-river.s: The Vakhsh is a river of Tajikistan, about 520 km long, formed by the Kyzylsu, which rises in Kyrgyzstan, and flowing south-west to join the Panj and form the Amu Darya. In the Soviet period it was harnessed by a cascade of dams, including the Nurek dam, and its lower valley…

vyachko.s: Vyachko was a Rus' prince of the Polotsk dynasty who ruled Koknese on the Daugava in present-day Latvia. Pressed by the Livonian crusaders, he ceded half his land to Bishop Albert of Riga in 1207, then burned Koknese and withdrew in 1208.

voronet-monastery.s: Voroneț is a monastery in Bukovina, north-eastern Romania, founded by Stephen the Great in 1488. Its exterior walls were painted in 1547 under Metropolitan Grigore Roșca, and its Last Judgement and intense blue pigment, known as 'Voroneț blue', made it the best known of the…

vereya.s: Vereya is a small town in Moscow Oblast, Russia, on the Protva river south-west of Moscow. First mentioned in the 14th century, it was an appanage of the Moscow princes under Andrei of Mozhaysk and his son Mikhail until it was absorbed by Moscow in 1486.

vsevolod-i-of-kiev.s: Vsevolod I, a son of Yaroslav the Wise, received Pereyaslavl on his father's death in 1054 and was Grand Prince of Kiev from 1078 to 1093. He married a Byzantine princess, said to be of the Monomachos family, and was the father of Vladimir Monomakh.

vitebsk.s: Vitebsk is a city in north-eastern Belarus on the Western Dvina. Recorded from the early 11th century as a town of the Polotsk lands, it became the seat of its own princes in the 12th century and passed to the Grand Duchy of Lithuania after Algirdas married the heiress of its…

vogt.s: Vogt (plural Vögte), from the Latin advocatus, was a German title for an official who protected and represented church lands and later, more generally, for a lord's or a king's administrator of a district, with judicial and fiscal powers. Some Vögte became territorial rulers…

varkhuman.s: Varkhuman was king of Samarkand in the mid-7th century. Tang China recognised him as ruler of Kangju around 658.

vathy-samos.s: Vathy is the main town and port of the Greek island of Samos, on a deep bay of its north-eastern coast. It grew in the 19th century and served as the capital of the autonomous Principality of Samos under Ottoman suzerainty, with the prince's residence and the island's assembly.

viseslav-of-serbia.s: Višeslav is the earliest Serbian ruler known by name, recorded by the Byzantine emperor Constantine VII Porphyrogennetos as a descendant of the leader who brought the Serbs to the Balkans. He is usually dated to around 780 and is regarded as the founder of the Vlastimirović…

vlastimir.s: Vlastimir was Prince of Serbia in the first half of the 9th century and the ruler who gave his name to the Vlastimirović dynasty. He united several Serbian tribes and defeated the Bulgarian khan Presian in a three-year war around 839 to 842.

vlore.s: Vlorë, historically Valona, is a port city in south-western Albania on the Bay of Vlorë. Ancient Aulon, it was contested in the Middle Ages by Byzantium, the Normans, the Serbian Empire and local lords before the Ottomans took it in 1417.

vyazma.s: Vyazma is a town in Smolensk Oblast, Russia, on the Vyazma river on the road from Moscow to Smolensk. Seat of a small principality from the 13th century, it was taken by Lithuania in 1403 and by Moscow in 1494.

vlad-the-impaler.s: Vlad III, known as Vlad the Impaler or Dracula, was voivode of Wallachia in 1448, from 1456 to 1462 and in 1476. Notorious for impaling enemies, he fought the Ottomans and in 1462 launched a night attack on the camp of Mehmed II, but was soon driven out and held prisoner in…

vladivostok.s: Vladivostok is a Russian port city on the Sea of Japan, near the borders with China and North Korea. Founded in 1860 as a military outpost after Russia gained the territory from China, it became the Pacific terminus of the Trans-Siberian Railway and the base of the Pacific Fleet.

vasco-de-quiroga.s: Vasco de Quiroga was a Spanish judge and churchman who became the first bishop of Michoacán in Mexico. Sent to New Spain as a judge of the second Audiencia in 1531, he founded hospital-villages for indigenous people inspired by Thomas More's Utopia, and as bishop from 1538 he…

valentinian-i.s: Valentinian I was Roman emperor from 364 to 375. A Pannonian officer acclaimed by the army after Jovian's death, he gave the East to his brother Valens and ruled the West himself, spending most of his reign fortifying the Rhine and Danube frontiers against the Alemanni, Quadi…

vannius.s: Vannius was a king of the Quadi installed by the Romans in 19 CE in the lands north of the middle Danube, roughly modern Slovakia and Moravia, after the fall of the Marcomannic rulers Maroboduus and Catualda. His client kingdom grew rich from raiding and tolls, but around 50…

vorma.s: The Vorma is a short river in eastern Norway that drains Lake Mjøsa south past Eidsvoll to join the Glomma at Nes in Romerike. Its valley, among the most fertile farmland in Norway, has been densely settled since prehistoric times.

vojvodina.s: Vojvodina is an autonomous province of northern Serbia, covering Bačka, the Serbian part of the Banat and most of Srem, with its capital at Novi Sad. Long part of the Kingdom of Hungary and the Habsburg lands, it took its name from the Serbian Vojvodina proclaimed in 1848.

velama.s: The Velamas are a Telugu-speaking landholding community of Andhra Pradesh and Telangana in southern India. Velama warrior families served the Kakatiya dynasty, and after its fall the Recherla Velamas ruled Telangana from Rachakonda and Devarakonda in the 14th and 15th centuries.

vilaine.s: The Vilaine is the longest river of Brittany in north-western France, flowing about 220 km from the department of Mayenne through Rennes, where it is joined by the Ille, to the Atlantic Ocean. Together with the Ille it gives its name to the department of Ille-et-Vilaine.

vemork.s: Vemork is a hydroelectric power station near Rjukan in Telemark, Norway, opened in 1911. During the German occupation its plant was the main source of heavy water for German nuclear research, and in February 1943 Norwegian commandos sabotaged it in Operation Gunnerside.

volksraad-dutch-east-indies.s: The Volksraad (People's Council) was an advisory and later partly legislative assembly of the Dutch East Indies, which first met in Batavia in 1918. Its members were partly elected by local councils and partly appointed, and included Indonesians, Europeans, and Chinese and…

volto-santo-of-lucca.s: The Volto Santo of Lucca is a large wooden crucifix showing Christ robed and alive on the cross, kept in a chapel in Lucca Cathedral. Legend held that it was carved by Nicodemus and came to Lucca miraculously in the 8th century; radiocarbon dating published in 2020 placed it…

val-dossola.s: The Val d'Ossola is an Alpine valley system in the north of Piedmont, Italy, drained by the river Toce and bordered on three sides by Switzerland. Its main town is Domodossola, and it carries the road and railway from Milan to the Simplon Pass.

visp.s: Visp is a town in the canton of Valais, Switzerland, at the confluence of the Vispa with the Rhône, at the entrance to the valleys leading to Zermatt and Saas-Fee. It was one of the seven tenths (Zenden) of the Republic of the Valais.

vet-river.s: The Vet River is a river of the Free State province of South Africa and a tributary of the Vaal. In the 1830s Voortrekker parties settled the land between the Vet and the Vaal, where the town of Winburg became the first Boer centre north of the Orange River.

volksraad.s: The Volksraad (Dutch for 'people's council') was the elected legislature of the Boer republics of southern Africa in the 19th century, including the Natalia Republic, the Orange Free State and the South African Republic. Its members were chosen by enfranchised white burghers,…

vicente-alvarez.s: Vicente Álvarez was a Filipino revolutionary general from Zamboanga who led the rising against the Spanish garrison there in 1899. After Spain withdrew in May 1899 he became president of the short-lived Republic of Zamboanga, but he was soon ousted by rival factions, and the…

vitus-bering.s: Vitus Bering was a Danish-born navigator in Russian service who led two great expeditions to the North Pacific. On the first, in 1728, he sailed through the strait between Asia and America that now bears his name; on the second he reached the coast of Alaska in 1741, but died…

valjala.s: Valjala is a village on the island of Saaremaa in Estonia, site of one of the island's main prehistoric strongholds. In early 1227 a crusader army crossed the frozen sea and captured the fort, forcing the islanders to accept baptism and completing the conquest of Estonia.

viljandi.s: Viljandi is a town in southern Estonia, on a lake in the old land of Sakala. Its hillfort was a chief stronghold of the Sakalians until German crusaders captured it in the 1210s and finally in 1224, after which the Livonian Brothers of the Sword built Fellin castle there, one…

var-river.s: The Var is a river of south-eastern France that flows about 114 kilometres from the Maritime Alps to the Mediterranean just west of Nice. In antiquity it formed the boundary between Gaul and Italy, and until 1860 its lower course marked the border between France and the County…

veracruz.s: Veracruz is a state of Mexico stretching along the Gulf of Mexico coast between Tamaulipas and Tabasco. Its tropical lowlands were home to the Olmec centres of San Lorenzo and Tres Zapotes, the Classic city of El Tajín and the Huastec and Totonac peoples.

veracruz-city.s: Veracruz is the principal Gulf of Mexico port of Mexico, in the state of the same name. Founded by Hernán Cortés in 1519 as the Villa Rica de la Vera Cruz and later moved to its present site, it was the gateway of New Spain through which the silver fleets sailed to Seville,…

veliko-tarnovo.s: Veliko Tarnovo is a city in north-central Bulgaria on the Yantra river, built on hills including Tsarevets and Trapezitsa. As Tarnovo it was the capital of the Second Bulgarian Empire from the Asen revolt of 1185 until its capture by the Ottomans in 1393, and a centre of…

viesturs.s: Viesturs was a ruler of the Semigallians in the early 13th century. He first allied with Bishop Albert of Riga and the German crusaders against the Lithuanians, then turned against the Germans as they pressed into Semigallia.

vasudeva.s: Vasudeva is a Hindu deity, originally a hero of the Vrishni clan of Mathura who was worshipped as a god and later merged with Krishna and identified with Vishnu. His cult, the Bhagavata religion, is attested from the 2nd century BCE, notably by the Heliodorus pillar at…

vidisha.s: Vidisha is a city in Madhya Pradesh, central India, on the Betwa river near Sanchi. Ancient Vidisha, at nearby Besnagar, was a major trading town of the Maurya and Shunga periods, where the Shunga prince Agnimitra governed and the Greek envoy Heliodorus raised his pillar…

vryburg.s: Vryburg is a town in North West Province, South Africa. It was founded in 1882 as the capital of the Republic of Stellaland, its name meaning 'free town', and became the seat of British Bechuanaland in 1885 before passing to the Cape Colony in 1895.

vishnu.s: Vishnu is one of the principal gods of Hinduism, worshipped as the preserver of the universe and, in Vaishnavism, as the supreme being. He is believed to descend to earth in avatars, among them the boar Varaha, Rama and Krishna, to restore cosmic order.

vladikavkaz.s: Vladikavkaz is the capital of North Ossetia–Alania, Russia, on the Terek River at the northern end of the Darial Pass. Founded as a Russian fortress in 1784, it guarded the Georgian Military Road across the Caucasus and became the administrative centre of the Terek region.

vajiralongkorn.s: Vajiralongkorn, also known as Rama X, has been king of Thailand since 2016, succeeding his father Bhumibol Adulyadej. Crowned in 2019, he has taken personal control of the Crown Property Bureau's assets and of some army units.

valtellina.s: The Valtellina is the valley of the upper Adda river in Lombardy, northern Italy, running east from Lake Como towards the Stelvio pass. The Three Leagues of the Grisons conquered it in 1512 and ruled it as a subject land; a Catholic rising and massacre of Protestants in 1620,…

vikramaditya-tomar.s: Vikramaditya Tomar was the last Tomara ruler of Gwalior, in central India. Besieged in Gwalior Fort by Ibrahim Lodi of the Delhi Sultanate, he surrendered in 1523 and became a Lodi noble.

vanua-balavu.s: Vanua Balavu is the largest island of the northern Lau group in eastern Fiji, a long, irregular island of limestone and volcanic rock with sheltered bays. In the 19th century its village of Lomaloma became the seat of the Tongan noble Enele Maʻafu and of the Tovata confederacy…

vanua-levu.s: Vanua Levu is the second-largest island of Fiji, lying north-east of Viti Levu, with Labasa and Savusavu as its main towns. In the 19th century its chiefdoms of Macuata, Bua and Cakaudrove were drawn into wars with Bau and with the Tongan noble Enele Maʻafu, who extended his…

velu-thampi-dalawa.s: Velu Thampi Dalawa was the chief minister, or dalawa, of the kingdom of Travancore from 1802 to 1809. After reforming its administration and finances, he clashed with the British Resident over the subsidy demanded under the treaty of 1805, and in 1809 he led an armed revolt…

vindolanda.s: Vindolanda was a Roman auxiliary fort in northern England, just south of Hadrian's Wall in Northumberland. Built around 85 CE, before the wall, it was garrisoned by auxiliary units of Tungrians and Batavians.

verkhovna-rada.s: The Verkhovna Rada, or Supreme Council, is the parliament of Ukraine, a single chamber of 450 deputies. It began as the Supreme Soviet of the Ukrainian SSR, and after the first competitive elections of 1990 it declared Ukraine's state sovereignty that July.

verona-manifesto.s: The Verona Manifesto was the programme adopted by the Republican Fascist Party at its congress in Verona in November 1943, after Mussolini's restoration as head of the German-backed Italian Social Republic. Its eighteen points promised a republic, the socialisation of industry…

valladolid.s: Valladolid is a city in northern Spain at the meeting of the Pisuerga and Esgueva rivers, capital of Castile and León. Developed by Count Pedro Ansúrez in the late 11th century, it became a favoured residence of the Castilian court, the seat of a high court and a university.

valladolid-yucatan.s: Valladolid is a city in the east of the Mexican state of Yucatán, founded by Francisco de Montejo the Nephew in 1543 at Chauaca and moved in 1545 to the Maya town of Saci. Built over Saci's temples, it became the Spanish centre of eastern Yucatán.

vastupala.s: Vastupala was a Jain minister of the Vaghela rulers of Gujarat, serving Viradhavala at Dholka with his younger brother Tejapala from about 1220. A capable administrator and general, he also defended Gujarat against outside attack.

viradhavala.s: Viradhavala was a Vaghela chief of Gujarat, son of Lavanaprasada, who with his father held real power under the last Chaulukya kings in the early 13th century. Ruling from Dholka, he relied on the brothers Vastupala and Tejapala as ministers.

vassakara.s: Vassakara was the chief minister of Ajatashatru, king of Magadha, in the 5th century BCE. Buddhist texts, including the Mahaparinibbana Sutta, record that he asked the Buddha whether the Vajjis could be defeated, and later accounts tell how he feigned exile among them and…

varahadeva.s: Varahadeva was a minister of the Vakataka king Harishena in the late 5th century. An inscription in Cave 16 at Ajanta records that he dedicated this large monastery to the Buddhist community, describing its paintings and its setting.

vatsagulma.s: Vatsagulma was the capital of the western branch of the Vakataka dynasty, in the Deccan of India, identified with modern Washim in Maharashtra. The branch was founded in the 4th century by Sarvasena, a son of Pravarasena I, and reached its height under Harishena in the late…

vidarbha.s: Vidarbha is the eastern region of Maharashtra state in India, around Nagpur and Amravati. An ancient kingdom of that name appears in the Mahabharata and other Sanskrit literature.

vindhyashakti.s: Vindhyashakti was the founder of the Vakataka dynasty, which rose in the Deccan of India in the mid-3rd century as the Satavahana dynasty broke up. He is known from a Vakataka inscription at Ajanta and from the Puranas, which name him as a Brahmin chief.

vijayasena.s: Vijayasena was the founder of the power of the Sena dynasty of Bengal. Rising from a base in western Bengal as the Pala Empire declined, he defeated the Varman dynasty of eastern Bengal and the Palas and made himself master of most of Bengal during a long reign.

vakpatiraja-poet.s: Vakpatiraja was a poet of the court of King Yashovarman of Kannauj in the 8th century, writing in Maharashtri Prakrit. His Gaudavaho ('The Slaying of the King of Gauda') celebrates Yashovarman's campaigns, including the defeat of a king of Magadha and Gauda.

vatican-museums.s: The Vatican Museums are the art and archaeological museums of the popes in Vatican City, begun in 1506 when Pope Julius II displayed the newly found statue of Laocoön. Their collections include classical sculpture, Egyptian and Etruscan antiquities, the Raphael Rooms and the…

vatican-radio.s: Vatican Radio is the broadcasting service of the Holy See, set up by Guglielmo Marconi and inaugurated by Pope Pius XI on 12 February 1931. Run for most of its history by the Jesuits, it broadcasts in dozens of languages worldwide.

vulca.s: Vulca was an Etruscan sculptor of Veii, the only Etruscan artist named in Roman literature. Pliny the Elder records that Tarquinius Priscus summoned him to Rome to make the terracotta cult statue of Jupiter for the temple on the Capitol.

velay.s: The Velay is a historic region of the Massif Central in south-central France, around Le Puy-en-Velay, named after the Gallic Vellavi. Under the bishops of Le Puy and local counts, it later formed part of the province of Languedoc under the French monarchy.

venda-people.s: The Venda (VhaVenda) are a Bantu-speaking people of the Soutpansberg mountains and the land north to the Limpopo, in South Africa's Limpopo province and parts of Zimbabwe. Their language is Tshivenda.

vannes.s: Vannes is a city on the Gulf of Morbihan in Brittany, north-western France, capital of the Morbihan department. As Darioritum it was the chief town of the Gallic Veneti, whose name it keeps.

vel-dhiv-roundup.s: The Vel' d'Hiv Roundup was a mass arrest of Jews in Paris on 16–17 July 1942, carried out by French police under the Vichy government at German request. About 13,000 people, including some 4,000 children, were seized; many were held in the Vélodrome d'Hiver cycling stadium…

vichy.s: Vichy is a spa town on the Allier in the Auvergne, central France, known since Roman times for its mineral springs. After the defeat of 1940 the French government settled there because of its many hotels, and parliament, meeting in its casino, voted full powers to Philippe…

velletri.s: Velletri is a town in the Alban Hills south-east of Rome, Italy. As Velitrae it was a Volscian town that Rome colonised several times in the 5th and 4th centuries BCE; a bronze tablet found there is the main surviving text in the Volscian language.

vilayet.s: A vilayet was a first-level province of the Ottoman Empire under the administrative system introduced by the Provincial Law of 1864, which replaced the older eyalets. Each was headed by a governor (vali) and divided into sanjaks and smaller districts.

vachutyan.s: The Vachutyans were an Armenian princely family of the 13th and 14th centuries, vassals of the Zakarid rulers of northern Armenia. They held lands in Aragatsotn, around the monasteries of Hovhannavank and Saghmosavank, which they rebuilt and endowed.

vushmgir.s: Vushmgir ibn Ziyar was the brother of Mardavij and ruler of the Ziyarid dynasty from 935 to 967. He held Gorgan and Tabaristan against the Buyids and the Samanids, shifting his allegiance between them, but lost the Jibal to the Buyids.
